description.text: Welcome to **Swift: Zero to Hero**. By the end of this course you will be able to write Swift with confidence, build apps for iPhone, iPad and Mac with SwiftUI, and ship one to real people through TestFlight and the App Store.
Swift is the language Apple's own apps are written in. It is fast, safe and friendly: it catches whole families of mistakes before your program ever runs, and it reads almost like plain English.
How the course works
The course has two halves.

items: **The Swift language** (chapters 1 to 4). You write code right here, in the editor on the right, and press **Run** to check it. Each lesson ends with a few tests. When they all pass, the lesson is done.
**Apple apps** (chapters 5 to 9). You move to Xcode on your Mac. Each lesson walks you through building something real, with a checklist to tick off and a short quiz.

description.text: What you need
For the first half, nothing but this page. Sign in with your Asteria account to run code and keep your progress.

For the second half you need a Mac with **Xcode 27**, which is free from the Mac App Store. To run your apps on your own iPhone you only need a free Apple Account. To use TestFlight, iCloud, in-app purchases and the App Store, you need the **Apple Developer Program** membership. Chapter 5 explains exactly what it gives you.

lessons.title: Hello, world

description.text: Every programmer's first program says hello. In Swift it is one line:

description.code: print("Hello, world!")

description.text: `print` is a **function**: a named piece of work you can ask Swift to do. You call it by writing its name followed by parentheses. Whatever you put inside the parentheses is what it works on. Here that is a **string**, a piece of text written between double quotes.
When the program runs, `print` writes the text out and moves to a new line. You can call it as many times as you like, and Swift runs the lines from top to bottom:

description.code:
print("First")
print("Second")

instructions.text: Change the program so it prints `Hello, world!` and then, on the next line, `I am learning Swift.`

tests.text: The first line printed should be `Hello, world!`.
The second line printed should be `I am learning Swift.`

hints: Each line of output needs its own `print`.
Check the punctuation: a comma and an exclamation mark in the first line, a full stop at the end of the second.

lessons.title: Comments

description.text: A **comment** is a note for people reading your code. Swift ignores it completely.
A comment that starts with `//` runs to the end of the line:

description.code:
// Greet the user
print("Hi!") // this prints Hi!

description.text: For longer notes, wrap the text in `/*` and `*/`. It can span as many lines as you like:

description.code:
/*
 This program prints a greeting.
 Later it will ask for a name.
 */

description.text: Comments are also a handy way to switch a line off without deleting it: put `//` in front of it, and Swift skips it.
Good comments explain **why** the code does something. The code itself already says **what** it does.

instructions.text: The program prints two lines, but only the first should appear. Turn the second `print` into a comment so it no longer runs, and add a comment of your own on its own line anywhere in the program.

lessons.seed:
print("This line stays.")
print("This line goes.")

tests.text: Your program should print `This line stays.`
Your program should not print `This line goes.`
The second `print` should be commented out.

description.text: Check what you have learned so far.

questions.question: What does `print("Hi")` do?

answers.text: It writes `Hi` out and moves to a new line.
It asks the person using the program to type `Hi`.
It stores the text `Hi` for later.

questions.why: `print` writes its text to the output and then starts a new line.

questions.question: In which order does Swift run these lines?
questions.why: Swift runs the lines of a program from top to bottom.

questions.question: Which of these is a comment?
questions.why: `//` starts a comment only outside a string. Inside quotes, it is just text.

chapters.title: Swift fundamentals
chapters.summary: Values, collections, decisions, functions and closures: the core of every Swift program.

lessons.title: Constants with let

description.text: Programs work with **values**: numbers, text, true-or-false answers. To use a value more than once, you give it a name.
In Swift you name a value with `let`:

description.code:
let city = "Lisbon"
print(city)

description.text: This makes a **constant** called `city` that holds the text `"Lisbon"`. Wherever you write `city` afterwards, Swift uses its value.
A constant can never change. If you try, Swift refuses to build your program:

description.code:
let city = "Lisbon"
city = "Porto" // error: cannot assign to value: 'city' is a 'let' constant

description.text: That sounds strict, but it is one of Swift's best habits. Most values in a program are set once and never change. Saying so with `let` makes your code easier to trust, and Swift tells you straight away if you change something by mistake.
**Naming:** Swift names use `camelCase`: start with a small letter, and start each following word with a capital, like `firstName` or `numberOfGuests`. Choose names that say what the value means.

instructions.text: Create a constant called `language` that holds the text `"Swift"`, then print it.

hints: Write `let`, then the name, then `=`, then the value in double quotes.
Then pass the name to `print`, without quotes: `print(language)`.

description.text: Some values do need to change: a score in a game, the number of items in a basket. For those, use `var` to make a **variable**:

description.code:
var lives = 3
lives = 2
print(lives) // 2

description.text: The first line creates the variable and gives it a starting value. The second line gives it a new value. From then on, `lives` is `2`.
You can use a variable's current value to work out its next one:

description.code:
var steps = 100
steps = steps + 50   // 150
steps += 50          // 200: a shorter way to write the same thing
steps -= 25          // 175

description.text: `+=` adds to a variable, `-=` subtracts from it.
**Which should you use?** Start with `let`. Change to `var` only when the value really has to change. If you write `var` and never change the value, Swift gives you a gentle warning suggesting `let`.

instructions.text: Create a variable called `score` that starts at `0`. Then add `10` to it, then add `5` more, and print it. The program should print `15`.

tests.text: You should change `score` after creating it, using `+=` or `=`.

description.text: Every value in Swift has a **type**, which says what kind of value it is and what you can do with it. The ones you will use every day are:
Usually you do not have to say the type. Swift works it out from the value. This is called **type inference**:

description.code:
let year = 2026        // Int
let price = 4.99       // Double
let title = "Swift"    // String
let isOpen = true      // Bool

description.text: You can also write the type yourself, after a colon. This is a **type annotation**:

description.code:
let year: Int = 2026
var temperature: Double = 21

description.text: Notice the second line: `21` on its own would be an `Int`, but the annotation tells Swift you want a `Double`, so it becomes `21.0`.
Once a name has a type, it keeps it. A `String` variable can only ever hold text. Swift checks this before your program runs, which is why a whole class of mistakes simply cannot happen in Swift.

instructions.text: Create three constants, each with a type annotation:

items: `year`, an `Int`, set to `2026`
`temperature`, a `Double`, set to `18.5`
`isLearning`, a `Bool`, set to `true`

tests.text: You should write each type yourself, with a colon.

lessons.title: Working with numbers

description.text: Swift does arithmetic with the symbols you would expect:

Look closely at the last two. When both numbers are `Int`, division gives a whole number and drops anything after the point: `7 / 3` is `2`. The **remainder** operator `%` gives what is left over: `7 % 3` is `1`.
With `Double` you get the fractional part:
Swift never mixes `Int` and `Double` silently. If you have one of each, convert one so they match:

description.code:
let minutes = 90
let hours = Double(minutes) / 60   // 1.5

description.text: Integer division and remainder are a useful pair. They split a total into whole groups and what is left over, like turning minutes into hours and minutes.

instructions.text: `totalMinutes` is `135`. Create two constants:

items: `hours`: how many whole hours are in `totalMinutes`
`minutes`: how many minutes are left over

instructions.text: Use `/` and `%` on `totalMinutes`. Then print them like this: `2 h 15 min`

tests.text: You should work them out with `/` and `%`, not type the answers.
Your program should print `2 h 15 min`.

hints: There are 60 minutes in an hour, so `totalMinutes / 60` gives whole hours.
To print several values on one line, you can write `print("\(hours) h \(minutes) min")`. The next lesson explains how that works.

description.text: A `String` is text. You can join strings with `+`:

description.code:
let first = "Grace"
let last = "Hopper"
let full = first + " " + last   // "Grace Hopper"

description.text: Most of the time, though, you will use **string interpolation**. Write `\(` and `)` inside a string, and put any value or expression between them. Swift puts the value into the text:

description.code:
let name = "Grace"
let year = 1906
print("\(name) was born in \(year).")
print("Next year is \(year + 1).")

description.text: Interpolation works with any type, not only strings, so you do not have to convert numbers first.
A few more useful things strings can do:

description.code:
let word = "Swift"
word.count          // 5, the number of characters
word.uppercased()   // "SWIFT"
word.isEmpty        // false
word.hasPrefix("Sw") // true

description.text: For text over several lines, use three double quotes:

description.code:
let poem = """
    Roses are red,
    Swift is fast.
    """

instructions.text: Using `name` and `age`, create a constant called `intro` with the text `Ada is 36 years old.`, built with string interpolation. Then print `intro`.

tests.text: You should use string interpolation, not type the name and age again.
Your program should print `Ada is 36 years old.`

description.text: A `Bool` is either `true` or `false`. You get one whenever you compare two values:

description.code:
3 > 2      // true
3 == 4     // false: == means "is equal to"
3 != 4     // true:  != means "is not equal to"
"a" < "b"  // true: strings compare alphabetically

description.text: The comparison operators are `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Be careful not to confuse `==` (compare) with `=` (assign).
You can combine `Bool` values:

head: Operator
Meaning
Example
rows: or: at least one is true

description.text: Parentheses make longer conditions clear:

description.code:
let age = 16
let withAdult = true
let canEnter = age >= 18 || (age >= 12 && withAdult)  // true

instructions.text: A person can drive if they are 18 or older, or if they are at least 16 **and** have a learner's permit. Using `age` and `hasPermit`, create a constant `canDrive` that is `true` exactly when the person can drive.

tests.text: With `age` 17 and a permit, `canDrive` should be `true`.
You should work `canDrive` out from `age` and `hasPermit`, with `||` and `&&`.

description.text: Because Swift never mixes types silently, you sometimes need to convert a value yourself. You do it by writing the type you want, with the value in parentheses:

description.code:
let whole = 7
let decimal = Double(whole)   // 7.0
let rounded = Int(9.99)       // 9: converting to Int drops the fraction
let text = String(42)         // "42"

description.text: `Int(9.99)` cuts off the fraction instead of rounding. To round to the nearest whole number, round the `Double` first:

description.code: let r = Int(9.99.rounded())   // 10

description.text: The most common conversion is working out an average, which needs `Double` division even when the inputs are whole numbers:

description.code:
let total = 17
let count = 4
let average = Double(total) / Double(count)   // 4.25

blocks.text: Turning text into a number, like `Int("42")`, is different, because the text might not be a number at all. Swift handles that with *optionals*, which you will meet soon.

instructions.text: Three test scores add up to `totalPoints`. Create a constant `average` with the exact average score as a `Double`, by converting `totalPoints` and `tests`.

Create `tax`: the tax on the subtotal.

questions.why: `let` makes a constant. `var` makes a variable you can change.

questions.question: What is the type of `price` here?
questions.why: `4` has no fractional part, so Swift infers `Int`. Write `4.0` or `let price: Double = 4` for a `Double`.

lessons.title: Arrays

description.text: An **array** holds an ordered list of values of one type. Write it with square brackets:

description.code: let planets = ["Mercury", "Venus", "Earth", "Mars"]

description.text: Swift infers the type `[String]`: an array of strings. Each item has a position called its **index**, counting from **zero**:

description.code:
planets[0]     // "Mercury"
planets[2]     // "Earth"
planets.count  // 4

description.text: The last index is always `count - 1`. Asking for an index that does not exist, like `planets[4]`, stops the program with an error, so check `count` when you are not sure.
To change an array, it must be a `var`. `append` adds to the end:

description.code:
var visited = ["Earth"]
visited.append("Moon")
visited += ["Mars", "Phobos"]   // adds several at once
visited.count                   // 4

description.text: An empty array needs its type written out, because there is nothing for Swift to infer from:

description.code:
var scores: [Int] = []
scores.isEmpty   // true

items: Create a variable `colors` holding `"red"`, `"green"` and `"blue"`, in that order.
Add `"gold"` to the end.
Create a constant `second` holding the second color, read from the array by its index.
Print `colors.count`.

tests.text: You should read `second` from the array by index.

hints: Indexes start at zero, so the second item is at index `1`.

description.text: Arrays come with many useful tools. Here are the ones you will reach for most:

description.code:
var queue = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"]

queue.contains("Ben")        // true
queue.insert("Zoe", at: 0)   // ["Zoe", "Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"]
queue.remove(at: 1)          // removes "Ana" and gives it back
queue.removeLast()           // removes "Cleo"
queue.first                  // the first item, if there is one
queue.reversed()             // the items in the opposite order

description.text: `sort()` puts an array in order where it stands. `sorted()` leaves it alone and gives you a sorted copy:

description.code:
var numbers = [5, 2, 9, 1]
let ordered = numbers.sorted()   // [1, 2, 5, 9], numbers is unchanged
numbers.sort()                   // numbers is now [1, 2, 5, 9]

description.text: This is a pattern you will see across Swift: a verb like `sort` changes the value itself, and the same word ending in *-ed* or *-ing* gives you a new value instead.
Numbers have a few extras:

description.code:
let marks = [70, 85, 92]
marks.min()   // 70
marks.max()   // 92

description.text: `first`, `min()` and `max()` give back an *optional*, because an empty array has no first, smallest or largest item. You will learn all about optionals soon. For now, `?? 0` gives a fallback value if there is nothing there: `marks.max() ?? 0`.

instructions.text: `scores` holds some results.

items: Create `ranked`: a copy of `scores` sorted from smallest to largest, leaving `scores` unchanged.
Create `best`: the highest score, using `max()` with `?? 0` as the fallback.
Create `hasPerfect`: `true` if `scores` contains `100`.

lessons.title: Dictionaries

description.text: A **dictionary** stores values by **key** instead of by position. Think of a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key) to find its meaning (the value).

description.code: var capitals = ["France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo", "Kenya": "Nairobi"]

description.text: Its type is `[String: String]`: string keys, string values. Look a value up with its key in square brackets:

description.code:
capitals["Japan"]     // "Tokyo"
capitals["Narnia"]    // nil: there is no such key

description.text: Because a key might not be there, a lookup gives an *optional*: either the value, or `nil` (nothing). Use `??` to supply a default:

description.code: let capital = capitals["Narnia"] ?? "Unknown"   // "Unknown"

description.text: Adding and changing use the same syntax. Setting a key to `nil` removes it:

description.code:
capitals["Peru"] = "Lima"       // adds a new pair
capitals["France"] = "Paris"    // replaces the value for an existing key
capitals["Kenya"] = nil         // removes the pair
capitals.count                  // 3

description.text: A dictionary has no order. Keys are unique: each key appears once, though the same value can appear under many keys.
Dictionaries can hold any types. A common one counts things:

description.code:
var stock: [String: Int] = ["apples": 6]
stock["apples", default: 0] += 3    // 9
stock["pears", default: 0] += 2     // 2: a missing key starts at the default

instructions.text: `stock` tracks how many of each fruit a shop has.

items: Add `"cherries"` with a count of `40`.
The shop sold 4 apples: take `4` from `"apples"`.
The shop stopped selling bananas: remove `"bananas"`.
Create `pears`: the number of pears, or `0` if there are none.

tests.text: `pears` should be `0`, worked out with `??` or `default:`.
You should look the pears up in `stock`.

hints: `stock["apples", default: 0] -= 4` subtracts in one step.
Setting a key to `nil` removes it.

lessons.title: Sets

description.text: A **set** is a collection of unique values with no order. Make one by writing the type, because square brackets alone make an array:

description.code:
var tags: Set<String> = ["swift", "ios", "swift"]
tags.count   // 2: the repeated "swift" is kept once

description.text: Sets shine in two jobs. The first is removing duplicates:

description.code:
let visits = ["Ana", "Ben", "Ana", "Cleo", "Ben"]
let people = Set(visits)   // {"Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"}, in some order

description.text: The second is checking membership quickly. `contains` on a set is fast however large it grows, while an array has to look at items one by one.
Sets can also be compared and combined:

description.code:
let monday: Set = ["Ana", "Ben", "Cleo"]
let tuesday: Set = ["Ben", "Dev"]

monday.union(tuesday)          // everyone: Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev
monday.intersection(tuesday)   // on both days: Ben
monday.subtracting(tuesday)    // Monday only: Ana, Cleo

description.text: Add with `insert` and remove with `remove`. To get the items in order, use `sorted()`, which gives back an array.

instructions.text: Two classes list the languages their students speak.

items: Create `either`: every language spoken in either class.
Create `both`: the languages spoken in both classes.
Create `onlyA`: an array, sorted alphabetically, of languages spoken only in `classA`.

lessons.seed:
let classA: Set = ["English", "Spanish", "Mandarin"]
let classB: Set = ["English", "Spanish", "Hindi", "Arabic"]

tests.text: You should use set operations, not list the languages yourself.

description.text: A **tuple** groups a few values together, even of different types, without making a new type for them. Write them in parentheses:
Naming the parts makes code much clearer:

description.code:
let size = (width: 1920, height: 1080)
size.width    // 1920

description.text: You can unpack a tuple into separate constants in one go. This is called **destructuring**:

description.code:
let (w, h) = size
print(w * h)   // 2073600

description.text: Tuples are perfect for small, short-lived groups, such as a function that gives back two things (you will do that in Functions). For anything bigger or longer-lived, you will use a `struct`, which you meet in Modelling with types.

items: Create a constant `book`: a tuple with named parts `title` (`"Dune"`) and `pages` (`412`).
Destructure it into two constants, `t` and `p`.
Print `Dune has 412 pages.` using `t` and `p`.

tests.text: Your program should print `Dune has 412 pages.`

Zoe's age, or a crash if there is none

answers.text: `sorted()` changes the array itself; `sort()` returns a sorted copy
`sort()` changes the array itself; `sorted()` returns a sorted copy

lessons.title: Decisions with if

description.text: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`:
The condition must be a `Bool`. Swift does not treat numbers as true or false, so `if count { }` is an error; write `if count > 0 { }`.
Add `else` for the other case, and `else if` to test more conditions in order. Swift takes the **first** branch whose condition is true and skips the rest:
When you only need to choose between two **values**, the **ternary operator** is a compact alternative: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

description.code:
let items = 1
let label = items == 1 ? "item" : "items"
print("\(items) \(label)")   // 1 item

description.text: Use it for short choices. When the logic grows, an `if` statement reads better.

instructions.text: Set `grade` to a letter based on `score`:

items: `90` or more: `"A"`
below `70`: `"F"`

instructions.text: Declare `grade` as `let grade: String` without a value, then give it its value in each branch. Swift checks that every path gives it exactly one value.

tests.text: With a score of `84`, `grade` should be `"B"`.

hints: Test the highest band first. Because Swift takes the first true branch, `score >= 80` then only catches 80 to 89.

description.text: `switch` compares one value against several **cases**, and runs the first that matches:

description.code:
let day = "Sat"
switch day {
case "Sat", "Sun":
    print("Weekend")
case "Fri":
    print("Almost there")
default:
    print("Weekday")
}

description.text: A few things make Swift's `switch` special:

items: **It must be exhaustive.** Every possible value has to be handled. For strings and numbers that means a `default` case.
**No fall-through.** Only the matching case runs, so there is no `break` to forget.
**Cases can match more than one value**, separated by commas.
**Cases can match ranges and conditions:**

description.code:
let speed = 72
switch speed {
case 0:
    print("Stopped")
case 1..<30:
    print("Slow")
case 30...70:
    print("Normal")
case let s where s > 120:
    print("Dangerous: \(s)")
default:
    print("Fast")
}

description.text: `1..<30` means 1 up to but not including 30. `30...70` includes both ends. `case let s where …` binds the value to a name and adds a condition.
`switch` can also give a value directly, which keeps things tidy:

instructions.text: Use a `switch` on `month` (1 to 12) to set `season`, for the northern hemisphere:

items: anything else: `"Unknown"`

tests.text: You should handle values outside 1 to 12 with `default`.

description.text: A `for-in` loop runs its body once for each item in a sequence:
Ranges are sequences too, so you can loop over numbers:
If you need both the position and the item, use `enumerated()`:
To count in steps, use `stride`:
Looping over a dictionary gives you each key and value as a tuple:

description.text: A `for-in` loop is right when you know what you are looping over. When you only know **when to stop**, use `while`. It checks its condition before each pass:

description.code:
var balance = 100.0
var years = 0
while balance < 200 {
    balance *= 1.07
    years += 1
}
print("Doubled in \(years) years")

description.text: `repeat-while` checks **after** each pass, so its body always runs at least once:
Two keywords steer any loop:

items: `continue` skips the rest of this pass and moves to the next.
`break` leaves the loop completely.

if x > 50 { print("big") } else if x > 70 { print("bigger") }

questions.question: Why does Swift's `switch` on a `String` need a `default` case?

answers.text: To catch mistakes in the case values
Because a `switch` must handle every possible value

description.text: A **function** is a named piece of code you can run whenever you need it. You have been calling `print` all along. Now you will write your own.
`func` starts the function, then comes its name and parentheses, then its body in braces. Defining a function does not run it; calling it with `sayHello()` does.
Functions become useful when they take **parameters** (inputs) and **return** a result (output):
`number: Int` is a parameter: a name and a type. `-> Int` says the function gives back an `Int`. `return` hands that value back to whoever called it, and ends the function.
When the body is a single expression, you can leave out `return`:
Good functions do one job and have a name that says what that job is. If you find yourself copying the same few lines, it is time for a function.

instructions.text: Write a function `greeting(name:)` that takes a `String` and returns `"Hello, <name>!"`. For example, `greeting(name: "Lin")` returns `"Hello, Lin!"`.
Then print `greeting(name: "Swift")`.

lessons.title: Argument labels

description.text: Swift functions read like sentences when you call them. That is thanks to **argument labels**.
Each parameter can have two names: a label used when **calling** the function, and a name used **inside** it.
Outside, the call reads "move from 3 to 10". Inside, the code uses the clearer `start` and `end`.
If you give a parameter one name, it is used for both. If you do not want a label at all, write `_`:

description.code:
func double(_ n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }
double(21)   // no label needed: it reads naturally

description.text: Apple's own APIs follow these habits, and you will see them everywhere:

items: Leave the first label out when the function name already says what it is: `names.append("Ana")`, not `append(item:)`.
Use prepositions to make calls read well: `insert("Ana", at: 0)`, `distance(from: a, to: b)`.

instructions.text: Write a function `distance(from:to:)` that takes two `Int` parameters and returns how far apart they are, always as a positive number. Inside the function, call the parameters `a` and `b`.
For example, `distance(from: 3, to: 10)` and `distance(from: 10, to: 3)` both return `7`.

tests.text: The parameters should have the labels `from` and `to`, and the names `a` and `b`.

hints: `abs(x)` gives the absolute value of `x`: it turns `-7` into `7`.

description.text: A parameter can have a **default value**. Callers can then leave it out:

Default values keep calls short for the common case while still allowing the unusual one. `print` uses them: it has hidden parameters `separator` and `terminator`, and `print("a", terminator: "")` prints without starting a new line.
A **variadic** parameter accepts any number of values, written with `...` after the type. Inside the function, it is an array:

items: Write `average(_:)`, which takes any number of `Double` values and returns their average. If there are none, return `0`.

Write `price(_:discount:)`, which takes a `Double` price and a `Double` discount that defaults to `0.1`, and returns the price after the discount. `price(50)` returns `45.0`, and `price(50, discount: 0.5)` returns `25.0`.

description.text: A function returns one value, but that value can be a tuple. This is how to give back several related results at once:
Because the tuple's parts are named in the return type, callers can use those names. They can also destructure the result:

description.code: let (first, last) = split("Alan Turing")

instructions.text: Write `stats(_:)`, which takes an array of `Int` and returns a tuple `(min: Int, max: Int, total: Int)`. You can assume the array is not empty.
For `[4, 9, 1, 7]` it returns `(min: 1, max: 9, total: 21)`.

checks.code:
let s = stats([4, 9, 1, 7])
expect(s.min == 1 && s.max == 9 && s.total == 21)

let s = stats([5])
expect(s.min == 5 && s.max == 5 && s.total == 5)

description.text: guard: leave early
`guard` checks that something is true, and if it is not, leaves straight away. Its `else` block must exit, usually with `return`:

`guard` keeps the main path of a function flush with the left edge, with problems handled at the top. Compare that with a pile of nested `if` statements, and you will see why Swift programmers love it. You will use it even more with optionals in the next module.
inout: change the caller's variable

Parameters are constants: a function cannot change what it is given. If a function really must change a variable that belongs to the caller, mark the parameter `inout`, and put `&` in front of the variable when calling:
The `&` makes the change visible at the call site. Use `inout` sparingly: returning a new value is usually clearer.

items: Write `shipping(weight:)`, taking a `Double` weight in kilograms and returning an `Int` cost. Use `guard` to return `0` for a weight of `0` or less. Otherwise it costs `5`, plus `2` more if the weight is over `10`.
Write `clamp(_:)` with an `inout Int` parameter that changes the value so it is never below `0` or above `100`.

checks.code:

clamp(&a); clamp(&b); clamp(&c)
expect(a == 100 && b == 0 && c == 40)

questions.question: What does `_` mean in `func double(_ n: Int)`?

answers.text: There is no argument label, so you call it `double(4)`

questions.why: `_` removes the label.

questions.question: What must a `guard … else { }` block do?

answers.text: Run the rest of the function
Leave the current scope, for example with `return`

questions.why: `guard` is for early exits, so Swift requires the `else` block to leave.

questions.question: What is the type of `numbers` inside `func sum(_ numbers: Int...)`?
questions.why: A variadic parameter arrives as an array.

questions.question: When is `inout` the right choice?

answers.text: Whenever a function returns more than one value
Whenever a function needs a parameter
Rarely: when a function must change a variable that belongs to its caller

questions.why: Returning a new value is usually clearer; `inout` is for the few cases where changing in place is the point.

description.text: Sometimes a value is simply not there. A person may have no middle name. Text typed into a form may not be a number. A dictionary may not have the key you asked for.

Many languages use a special "null" value for this, and programs crash when they forget to check for it. Swift's answer is the **optional**: a type that says "either a value, or nothing", where nothing is written `nil`.
You make a type optional by adding `?`:

description.code:
var middleName: String? = nil   // no middle name yet
middleName = "Marie"            // now there is one

description.text: `String?` and `String` are different types. A `String` is always text. A `String?` might be text or `nil`, and Swift will not let you use it as text until you have checked. That check is what prevents the crashes.
You have already met optionals without knowing it:

description.code:
let maybeNumber = Int("42")     // Int?: 42
let notNumber = Int("forty")    // Int?: nil
let first = [Int]().first       // Int?: nil, the array is empty

description.text: `Int("42")` gives an `Int?`, because not every piece of text is a number.
Printing an optional shows it wrapped, like `Optional(42)`, which is a reminder that you have not looked inside yet. The next lessons show how to look inside safely.

items: Create a variable `nickname` of type `String?` that starts as `nil`.
Create a constant `parsed` from `Int("2026")`.
Create a constant `failed` from `Int("twenty")`.

tests.text: You should declare `nickname` with `var` and the type `String?`.

description.text: To use the value inside an optional, you **unwrap** it. The everyday way is `if let`:
`if let` checks for a value. If there is one, it binds it to a new constant, without the `?`, which you can use inside the braces. If there is not, the `else` branch runs.
When the unwrapped value can have the same name as the optional, there is a shorter form:
You can unwrap several optionals at once, and add conditions, separated by commas. Everything must succeed for the body to run:

instructions.text: Write `describe(_:)`, which takes an `Int?` age and returns:

items: `"Age not given"` if it is `nil`,
`"Age <n>"` otherwise, like `"Age 34"`.

instructions.text: Use `if let`.

description.text: `guard let` unwraps an optional and, if it is `nil`, leaves straight away. If it succeeds, the unwrapped value stays available for the **rest of the function**, not just inside braces:
Use `guard let` when the function cannot do its real work without the value. Use `if let` when the value is a nice extra.
Functions that might not be able to produce a result often return an optional themselves:

instructions.text: Write `parseAge(_:)`, which takes a `String` and returns an `Int?`:

items: If the text is not a whole number, return `nil`.
If the number is below `0` or above `130`, return `nil`.
Otherwise return the number.

description.text: Nil-coalescing: ??
`??` unwraps an optional or uses a fallback if it is `nil`. The result is never optional:

description.code:
let saved: Int? = nil
let volume = saved ?? 50     // 50, a plain Int

description.text: You can chain them to try several sources in order:

description.code: let theme = userTheme ?? teamTheme ?? "light"

description.text: Optional chaining: ?.
If you want something **from** an optional, put `?` before the dot. If the optional is `nil`, the whole expression quietly becomes `nil` instead of crashing:

description.code:
let nickname: String? = "Ace"
let length = nickname?.count       // Int?: 3
let shout = nickname?.uppercased() // String?: "ACE"

description.text: Because the result is still optional, chaining pairs naturally with `??`:

description.code: let letters = nickname?.count ?? 0

Create `nameLength`: the number of characters in `settings["name"]`, or `0` if there is no name, using `?.` and `??`.

lessons.title: Force unwrapping, and why to avoid it

description.text: There is one more way to unwrap: `!`, the **force unwrap**. It says "I am certain there is a value. Give it to me."

description.code: let number = Int("42")!   // 42

description.text: If you are wrong, the program crashes on the spot:

description.code: let oops = Int("forty")!   // Fatal error: Unexpectedly found nil

description.text: Every `!` is a promise to Swift that it cannot check. Experienced Swift programmers keep them rare and only use one when a `nil` would mean a bug in their own code, never because of what a user typed or a server sent. Even then, a message makes the crash easier to understand:
When in doubt, use `if let`, `guard let` or `??`.

items: `total` adds up only the inputs that are valid numbers, and
`invalid` counts the inputs that are not.

description.text: Five questions on optionals.

questions.question: What is the type of `Int("12")`?
questions.why: Not all text is a number, so the conversion gives an optional.

questions.question: What does `nickname ?? "friend"` give when `nickname` is `nil`?

questions.question: What is `name?.count` when `name` is `"Ana"`?
questions.why: Optional chaining always produces an optional, even when there is a value.

questions.question: When should you choose `guard let` over `if let`?

answers.text: When the function cannot do its main job without the value

questions.why: `guard let` leaves early and keeps the unwrapped value for the rest of the function.

questions.question: What happens when you force unwrap `nil` with `!`?

description.text: In Swift, functions are values. You can store one in a constant, pass it to another function, or return it, like a number or a string.
A **closure** is a function written without a name, right where you need it. It goes in braces, with its parameters and return type before the word `in`:

description.code:
let double = { (n: Int) -> Int in
    return n * 2
}

double(21)   // 42

description.text: The type of `double` is `(Int) -> Int`: a function that takes an `Int` and returns an `Int`. You can write that type yourself, which also lets Swift infer the closure's parameter types:

description.code: let triple: (Int) -> Int = { n in n * 3 }

description.text: As with functions, a closure made of one expression returns that expression without `return`.
A named function can be used in the same places:

items: Create a closure constant `isEven` of type `(Int) -> Bool` that returns `true` for even numbers.
Create a closure constant `join` of type `(String, String) -> String` that joins two strings with a space between them.

tests.text: `isEven` and `join` should be closures stored with `let`.

description.text: Closures are most useful when you hand them to another function, which calls them when it needs to. Here, `repeatTwice` takes a closure as its parameter:
`() -> Void` means a closure that takes nothing and returns nothing.
When a closure is the **last** argument, you can write it after the parentheses. This is **trailing closure** syntax, and it is everywhere in Swift and SwiftUI:
Swift also lets you shorten closures a lot. These all mean the same thing:
Use the short forms when the closure is tiny and obvious. When it is longer, name the parameters.

items: Write `applyTwice(_:to:)`, which takes a closure of type `(Int) -> Int` and a starting `Int`, and returns the result of applying the closure twice. `applyTwice({ $0 + 3 }, to: 1)` returns `7`.
Create `byLength`: `words` sorted from shortest to longest, using `sorted` with a trailing closure.

tests.text: You should use a trailing closure with `sorted`.

description.text: Three closure-taking methods do much of the everyday work on collections. Each one replaces a hand-written loop with a single, clear line.
**`map`** transforms every item and gives you a new array:

description.code:
let prices = [4.0, 10.0, 2.5]
let withTax = prices.map { $0 * 1.2 }   // [4.8, 12.0, 3.0]
let labels = prices.map { "£\($0)" }    // the type can change too

description.text: **`filter`** keeps the items for which the closure returns `true`:

description.code: let cheap = prices.filter { $0 < 5 }    // [4.0, 2.5]

description.text: **`reduce`** combines every item into one value. You give it a starting value and a closure that adds one item to the running result:

description.code:
let total = prices.reduce(0, +)                  // 16.5
let longest = ["a", "abc", "ab"].reduce("") { $0.count >= $1.count ? $0 : $1 }

description.text: Two relatives are worth knowing straight away:

description.code:
let numbers = ["1", "two", "3"].compactMap { Int($0) }  // [1, 3]: drops the nils
let anyFree = prices.contains { $0 == 0 }               // false

description.text: They chain together into a short story about your data:

description.code: let result = prices.filter { $0 > 3 }.map { $0 * 2 }.reduce(0, +)   // 28.0

instructions.text: `orders` is a list of order amounts. Using `map`, `filter`, `reduce` and `compactMap`:

items: `bigOrders`: the orders over `100`.
`doubled`: every order multiplied by `2`.
`revenue`: the sum of all orders.
`codes`: the numbers that can be read from `rawCodes`, skipping any that are not numbers.

description.text: A closure can use constants and variables from around where it was written. It **captures** them, keeping them alive as long as the closure lives.
`count` belongs to `makeCounter`, which has finished running, yet the closure still reaches it. Each call to `makeCounter` makes a fresh `count`, captured by a fresh closure.
This is what lets a button in an app remember what to do when it is tapped long after the code that set it up has run.

blocks.text: When a closure is stored to be called later, Swift marks the parameter `@escaping`. You will see it in function signatures like `func onTap(_ action: @escaping () -> Void)`. It reminds you the closure outlives the call, and it matters when you learn about memory in Classes.

instructions.text: Write `makeAccumulator(start:)`, which takes an `Int` and returns a closure of type `(Int) -> Int`. Each time the closure is called with a number, it adds that number to a running total, which begins at `start`, and returns the new total.

tests.text: An accumulator starting at `10` should give `15`, then `18`.
Two accumulators should keep separate totals.

description.text: A teacher keeps marks for each student in a dictionary. Use closures to answer questions about the class, without writing a single `for` loop.

items: `averages`: a `[String: Double]` with each student's average mark. Use `mapValues`, which works like `map` on a dictionary's values.
`honours`: an alphabetically sorted array of the students whose average is `85` or more.
`classAverage`: the average of every single mark in the class, as a `Double`. `marks.values.flatMap { $0 }` gives you one array of all the marks.
`report`: one line per student, sorted by name, like `"Ana: 91.0"`, joined with new lines. Use `.joined(separator: "\n")`.

questions.question: What is the type of `{ (a: Int, b: Int) in a + b }`?

questions.question: What does `[1, 2, 3].map { $0 * 10 }` give?

questions.why: `compactMap` drops every `nil` result.

questions.question: Why does each call to a `makeCounter()` function get its own count?

answers.text: Each call creates a new variable, which its own closure captures
Swift resets the count every time

questions.why: Captured variables live as long as the closure that captured them.

description.text: In this workshop you will build a word-guessing game, one step at a time. The player guesses letters; correct letters are revealed, and too many wrong guesses lose the game.
Every step starts from the code you finished in the step before. Each one adds a single new piece, so you can see a real program grow.
A game is mostly **state**: the things it has to remember. Ours needs three:

items: the secret word,
the letters guessed so far,
how many guesses were wrong.

instructions.text: Create:

a variable `guessed`, an empty `Set<Character>`,
a variable `wrongGuesses`, starting at `0`,
a constant `maxWrong` set to `6`.

`wrongGuesses` should be a variable starting at `0`.

lessons.title: Step 2: showing the word

Looping over a `String` gives you each `Character`. For each one, show it if it has been guessed, or `_` if not. Then join the pieces with spaces.
Collecting into an array of strings and calling `joined(separator: " ")` is a neat way to put spaces between the pieces but not at the end.

lessons.title: Step 5: playing a game

description.text: Time to play. Here, the player's guesses arrive as a string of letters, one guess per letter. Loop over them, make each guess, and print what happened.
Stop as soon as the game is won or lost, even if there are guesses left. `break` leaves a loop early.

For each letter in `guesses`, makes the guess and prints `"<letter>: <masked>"`, like `S: S _ _ _ _`. Use the letter exactly as given.
After each guess, if the game is won, prints `You win!` and stops. If it is lost, prints `Out of guesses. It was SWIFT.` and stops.

instructions.text: Then call `play("sxwift")`.

checks.code:
^s: S _ _ _ _
x: S _ _ _ _
w: S W _ _ _
i: S W I _ _
f: S W I F _
t: S W I F T
You win!$

description.text: You built a complete game from state, a few small functions and a loop. Look back over your code: each function does one job, and its name says which. That is the shape most good programs have, from games to apps.

So `"w"` and `"W"` count as the same guess
