chapters.title: Modelling with types
chapters.summary: Structs, classes, enums, protocols and generics: how Swift programs are shaped.

description.text: So far you have used Swift's types: `Int`, `String`, arrays. Real programs are about real things: books, songs, players, orders. A **struct** lets you make your own type that groups everything about one thing.

`title`, `author` and `pagesRead` are **properties**. Each `Book` has its own copy of them. Swift writes an initializer for you, called the **memberwise initializer**, with a parameter for each property:
Two kinds of "constant" are at work here:

items: A `let` **property** can never change once the book is made.
A struct stored in a `let` **constant** cannot change at all, not even its `var` properties:

description.code:
let fixed = Book(title: "Emma", author: "Jane Austen", pagesRead: 10)
fixed.pagesRead = 20   // error: 'fixed' is a 'let' constant

description.text: Type names start with a capital letter (`Book`); property and variable names start with a small one (`pagesRead`).

items: Define a struct `Song` with three properties: `title` (`String`, constant), `artist` (`String`, constant) and `plays` (`Int`, variable).
Create a variable `song` for `"Freely Given"` by `"Asteria Technology"` with `0` plays.
Add `1` to its plays twice.

tests.text: `Song` should be a struct with `title`, `artist` and `plays`.

checks.code:
let s = Song(title: "A", artist: "B", plays: 3)
expect(s.title == "A" && s.artist == "B" && s.plays == 3)

tests.text: `title` and `artist` should be constants, and `plays` a variable.

description.text: Functions that belong to a type are called **methods**. Inside a method, the type's properties are available by name:
A method that **changes** a struct's properties must be marked `mutating`. This is a promise Swift can check: only `mutating` methods change things, and they can only be called on a `var`:
When you need to be explicit, `self` means "this instance": `self.width`. It is mostly optional, but you will need it when a parameter has the same name as a property.

instructions.text: Complete `Counter`:

items: `increment()` adds `1` to `count`.
`reset()` sets `count` back to `0`.
`isOver(_ limit: Int) -> Bool` returns whether `count` is greater than `limit`.

instructions.text: Mark only the methods that change `count` as `mutating`.

tests.text: `reset()` should set the count to zero.
`isOver(2)` should be `true` when the count is 3.
`increment` and `reset` should be `mutating`, and `isOver` should not.

lessons.title: Initializers

description.text: An **initializer** sets up a new instance, giving every property its first value. You have been using the free memberwise one. Write your own with `init` when you want a friendlier or safer way to make values:
Rules worth knowing:

items: Every property must have a value by the end of `init`. Swift checks this for you.
A property can have a default value right where it is declared, like `var count = 0`. Then initializers do not have to set it.
Writing your own `init` inside the struct replaces the free memberwise one. To keep both, write yours in an **extension** instead, which you will meet soon.

description.text: An initializer can also fail, by being written `init?`. It returns an optional, and `return nil` means "no value could be made":

instructions.text: Write a struct `Duration` with one stored property, `seconds` (`Int`), and two initializers:

items: `init(seconds: Int)`
`init(minutes: Int, seconds: Int)`, which stores the total number of seconds.

instructions.text: Then add a failable initializer `init?(text: String)` that reads text like `"3:20"` (minutes and seconds) and returns `nil` if either part is not a number. `text.split(separator: ":")` gives you the parts.

hints: One initializer can call another with `self.init(...)`.

lessons.title: Computed properties and observers

description.text: Not every property needs to be stored. A **computed property** works out its value each time you read it, from other properties:
Computed properties are always `var`, and they are perfect for anything you would otherwise have to remember to update.
A stored property can run code when it changes, with a **property observer**. `didSet` runs after the change and can see the old value as `oldValue`:
There is also `willSet`, which runs just before a change, with the coming value as `newValue`. In SwiftUI apps you will mostly let the framework react to changes, but observers are handy in models.

instructions.text: Complete `Rectangle`:

items: A computed property `area` (width × height).
A computed property `isSquare` (`Bool`).
Give `width` a `didSet` observer that stops it going below `0`: if it is set to a negative value, set it to `0`.

tests.text: `isSquare` should be `true` only when the sides match.
`area` should update when a side changes.
Setting `width` below zero should make it `0`.

lessons.title: Value types and static members

description.text: Structs are values
Structs are **value types**. Assigning one to another variable, or passing it to a function, makes an independent **copy**:

description.code:
var a = Rectangle(width: 1, height: 1)
var b = a        // b is a copy
b.width = 10
a.width          // still 1

description.text: This is the same as with `Int` or `String`: changing one copy never surprises you by changing another. It is a big reason Swift code is easy to reason about, and why Swift's own `Array`, `Dictionary` and `String` are structs too.
Static members belong to the type
A `static` property or method belongs to the type itself, not to any one instance. Use it for shared constants and handy ready-made values:
When Swift already knows the type, you can drop its name and write just `.white`. You will do that constantly in SwiftUI: `.foregroundStyle(.blue)`.

items: Add a `static let origin` to `Point`, at `(0, 0)`.
Create `start` as `Point.origin`, then `moved` as a copy of `start`, and change `moved.x` to `5`.
Show that `start` is unchanged by creating `startX` from `start.x`.

tests.text: `moved.x` should be `5` and `startX` should still be `0`.

lessons.title: Lab: a recipe scaler

description.text: Recipes are written for a certain number of people. Build a small model that scales a recipe to feed any number.

items: A struct `Ingredient` with `name` (`String`), `amount` (`Double`) and `unit` (`String`).
A struct `Recipe` with `name` (`String`), `serves` (`Int`) and `ingredients` (`[Ingredient]`).
`Recipe` has a method `scaled(toServe people: Int) -> Recipe` that returns a new recipe for `people`, with every amount scaled in proportion. It does not change the original.
`Recipe` has a computed property `shoppingList: [String]`, with one line per ingredient like `"200.0 g flour"`.

tests.text: Scaling a recipe for 4 to 6 people should multiply each amount by 1.5.
Scaling should not change the original.

checks.code:
let r = Recipe(name: "Pancakes", serves: 4, ingredients: [Ingredient(name: "flour", amount: 200, unit: "g"), Ingredient(name: "eggs", amount: 2, unit: "whole")])
expect(r.shoppingList == ["200.0 g flour", "2.0 whole eggs"])

hints: Because structs are values, `var copy = self` gives you a copy to change and return.

description.text: Five questions on structs.

questions.question: Why must a method be marked `mutating` to change a property?

answers.text: So Swift knows which methods change the value, and can stop them being called on a `let`
Because methods cannot see properties otherwise

questions.why: `mutating` is a promise Swift checks: constants can only use non-mutating methods.

questions.question: After `var b = a; b.score = 10`, where `a` is a struct, what is `a.score`?

answers.text: Whatever it was before: `b` is a separate copy

questions.why: Structs are value types. Assigning one copies it.

questions.question: What is a computed property?

answers.text: A property whose value is worked out from other values each time it is read
A property that can only be set once
A property shared by every instance

questions.why: Computed properties store nothing; they calculate.

questions.question: What does `init?` mean?

answers.text: An initializer that can be skipped
An initializer that can fail and give `nil`

questions.why: A failable initializer returns an optional instance.

questions.question: How do you use a `static let shared` on a type `Settings`?
questions.why: Static members belong to the type, so you reach them through the type's name.

description.text: A **class** looks a lot like a struct: properties, methods, initializers. The big difference is what happens when you copy one.
Structs are values: copying makes an independent copy. Classes are **reference types**: copying gives you a second **reference** to the **same** object.
Notice two more differences:

items: **Classes have no free memberwise initializer.** You write `init` yourself (unless every property has a default value).
**No `mutating`.** `mine` is a `let`, yet its balance changed. The constant holds the *reference*, which cannot change; the object it points to can.

description.text: References are exactly right when something has an identity and is shared: one bank account seen from several screens, one music player the whole app controls. For plain data, prefer structs.

items: Define a class `Lamp` with a variable `isOn` (`Bool`) and an initializer that takes it.
Create a constant `hallLamp` that is off.
Create a constant `sameLamp` from `hallLamp`, then switch `sameLamp` on.

instructions.text: `hallLamp.isOn` should then be `true`, because both names refer to one lamp.

tests.text: `hallLamp` should be on after switching `sameLamp` on.
`hallLamp` and `sameLamp` should be the very same object.

description.text: A class can **inherit** from another. The new class, the **subclass**, gets everything its **superclass** has, and can add more or change behaviour:

items: `class Bicycle: Vehicle` means Bicycle inherits from Vehicle.
A subclass initializer sets its own properties first, then calls `super.init`.
`override` replaces a superclass method. Swift insists on the word, so you never override something by accident.
`super.describe()` calls the superclass's version.

blocks.text: Give a superclass an explicit `init`, even an empty `init() {}`. Without one, Swift 6 with Xcode's default settings can report that an initializer "has different actor isolation" from the one it overrides. You will learn what actor isolation means in Concurrency.

description.text: Mark a class `final` when nothing should inherit from it. Swift programmers often make classes `final` by default, and prefer protocols (coming soon) for sharing behaviour between types.

items: Define `Shape` with an empty `init()`, a method `area() -> Double` that returns `0`, and a method `describe() -> String` that returns `"Area: <area>"`, using `area()`.
Define `Circle`, a subclass of `Shape` with a `radius` (`Double`), that overrides `area()` to return `3.14 * radius * radius`.
Make `Circle` `final`.

tests.text: `describe()` on a circle should use the circle's area.
`Circle` should be `final`, inherit from `Shape`, and override `area`.

lessons.title: Memory and ARC

description.text: Every object a class makes takes up memory, and that memory must be freed when the object is no longer needed. Swift does this automatically with **Automatic Reference Counting**, or ARC.

ARC counts how many references point at each object. When the count drops to zero, nothing can reach the object any more, so Swift frees it straight away, and runs its **deinitializer**, `deinit`, if it has one:
Making the variable optional lets you set it to `nil`, which removes its reference.

This is predictable and immediate, with no pauses while a garbage collector runs, which is part of why Swift apps feel smooth. Most of the time you never think about it. The one case you do need to think about is in the next lesson.

items: Give `Session` a `deinit` that prints `Session <name> ended`.
Create a variable `session` of type `Session?`, set to a session named `"demo"`.
Set `session` to `nil`.

instructions.text: Your program should print the start message and then the end message.

tests.text: Your program should print `Session demo started` then `Session demo ended`.

lessons.title: Retain cycles, weak and unowned

description.text: ARC frees an object when nothing points at it. But what if two objects point at **each other**?
Each holds the other, so neither count ever reaches zero. This is a **retain cycle**, and it is a memory leak: the objects live forever.
The fix is to make one direction **weak**. A `weak` reference does not count. When the object it points at is freed, it becomes `nil` by itself, so it must be an optional `var`:
The rule of thumb: the "parent" holds the "child" strongly, and the child points back weakly.
`unowned` is like `weak` but not optional. Use it only when the other object is certain to outlive this one.
Closures can make cycles too
A closure stored by an object captures what it uses, including `self`, strongly. Break the cycle with a **capture list**:
You will see `[weak self]` in many codebases. With SwiftUI and Swift's modern concurrency you need it less often, but knowing why it exists is essential.

instructions.text: The code below leaks: the person and the pet keep each other alive. Change **one** property to `weak` so that setting both variables to `nil` frees them both, and both messages print.

tests.text: Your program should print both `Person freed` and `Pet freed`.

lessons.title: Struct or class?

description.text: You now know both. How do you choose? Apple's own advice is short: **use a struct by default**. Reach for a class when you need what only a class gives you.

head: Choose a struct when…
Choose a class when…
rows: It is plain data: a song, a point, an order
It has an identity that is shared: one player, one connection
Everyone should see the same changes
You want Swift to guarantee nobody changes it behind your back
You need inheritance, or `deinit` to clean up

description.text: In SwiftUI apps you will mostly write structs: every view is a struct. Your app's shared **model** will often be a class marked `@Observable`, so that every screen sees the same data and updates when it changes. You will meet that in the SwiftUI chapter.
A quick test you can apply: "If I copy this, should changing the copy change the original?" If no, struct. If yes, class.

instructions.text: Two types are half-written. Make `Note` a **struct** (plain data that is copied freely) and `NoteStore` a **class** (one shared store that everything uses). Then:

items: Create a `let store = NoteStore()`.
Add a note with the text `"Buy milk"` to `store.notes`.
Create `copy` from that note, change `copy.text` to `"Buy oat milk"`, and check the stored note is unchanged.

tests.text: `Note` should be a struct and `NoteStore` a class.
The store should hold one note reading `"Buy milk"`.

description.text: Five questions on classes and memory.

questions.question: `a` and `b` refer to the same class instance. You change `b.name`. What happens to `a.name`?

answers.text: It stays the same: `b` is a copy
It changes too: they are one object
Swift stops you with an error

questions.why: Classes are reference types; copying the reference shares the object.

questions.question: When does ARC free a class instance?

answers.text: As soon as no strong references point at it

questions.why: ARC counts strong references and frees the object when the count reaches zero.

questions.question: Two objects hold strong references to each other. What is this called?
questions.why: Neither count can reach zero, so neither object is freed.

questions.question: Why must a `weak` property be an optional `var`?

answers.text: It becomes `nil` by itself when the object it points at is freed

questions.why: Swift sets a weak reference to `nil` when its object goes away.

questions.question: Which should usually be your first choice for a new type?
questions.why: Prefer structs; reach for classes when you need shared identity, inheritance or `deinit`.

description.text: An **enum**, short for enumeration, is a type with a fixed set of possible values, called **cases**:
Enums make impossible values impossible. A `heading` can only ever be one of four directions. Compare that with a `String`, where a typo like `"nrth"` would slip through.
`switch` and enums are made for each other. Because Swift knows every case, a `switch` that covers them all needs no `default`:
And if you later add a case to the enum, Swift points at every `switch` that now needs updating. Leaving out `default` on purpose gets you that safety.

items: Define an enum `TrafficLight` with the cases `red`, `amber` and `green`.
Write `next(_:)`, which takes a `TrafficLight` and returns the one that follows it: red → green → amber → red.
Use a `switch` with no `default`.

tests.text: The light after `red` should be `green`, after `green` should be `amber`, and after `amber` should be `red`.
You should switch over every case without `default`.

description.text: Cases can carry a fixed **raw value** of one type, such as `String` or `Int`:
For `String` raw values, a case with no explicit value uses its own name: `case tea` has the raw value `"tea"`.
You can go the other way with `init(rawValue:)`. Not every value matches a case, so it gives an optional:

description.code:
Size(rawValue: "M")    // .medium
Size(rawValue: "XL")   // nil

description.text: Add `CaseIterable` and Swift gives you `allCases`, an array of every case in order. It is perfect for menus and pickers:
`\.rawValue` is a **key path**: a short way to say "the `rawValue` property of each item".

items: Define an enum `Weekday` with an `Int` raw value and `CaseIterable`, with cases `monday` through `sunday`, where `monday` is `1`.
Create `weekendNumbers`: the raw values of `saturday` and `sunday` in an array.
Create `fromNumber`: the weekday with raw value `3`, as an optional.
Create `count`: how many weekdays there are, from `allCases`.

description.text: Raw values are fixed. **Associated values** are different: each case can carry its own data, and each instance can carry different data.
To get the data back out, match the case in a `switch` and bind the values with `let`:
`_` ignores a value you do not need, and `where` adds a condition, as with numbers.
To check for one case only, use `if case`:
This is one of Swift's most powerful ideas. Together with `switch`, it lets you model "one of these, with exactly this data" precisely, and the compiler checks you handle every possibility.

items: Define an enum `Shape` with three cases: `circle(radius: Double)`, `rectangle(width: Double, height: Double)` and `square(side: Double)`.
Write `area(of:)`, which returns the area as a `Double`. Use `Double.pi` for π.

tests.text: The area of a `.rectangle(width: 3, height: 4)` should be `12`.
The area of a `.square(side: 5)` should be `25`.
The area of a `.circle(radius: 1)` should be π.

description.text: Enums can have methods and computed properties, just like structs. This makes them ideal for modelling **state**: the situation something is in, with the data that belongs to each situation.
Think about loading something from the internet. It is idle, or loading, or finished with data, or failed with an error message. Here is a version with separate properties:

description.code:
var isLoading = false
var data: [String]? = nil
var errorMessage: String? = nil

description.text: Nothing stops `isLoading` being `true` while `errorMessage` is set, which makes no sense. As an enum, impossible combinations cannot exist:
A method that changes `self` on an enum is `mutating`, as on a struct:
You will use exactly this pattern to drive screens in SwiftUI.

instructions.text: Define an enum `Order` that models a delivery: `placed`, `shipped(trackingNumber: String)`, `delivered(day: String)`, and `cancelled`.
Give it:

items: A computed property `summary: String`:
`placed`: `"Order placed"`
`shipped`: `"Shipped, tracking <number>"`
`delivered`: `"Delivered on <day>"`
`cancelled`: `"Cancelled"`
A computed property `canCancel: Bool`, `true` only while the order is placed.
A `mutating func ship(trackingNumber: String)` that changes a placed order to shipped and leaves any other state alone.

checks.code:
expect(Order.placed.summary == "Order placed")
expect(Order.shipped(trackingNumber: "Z9").summary == "Shipped, tracking Z9")
expect(Order.delivered(day: "Friday").summary == "Delivered on Friday")
expect(Order.cancelled.summary == "Cancelled")

tests.text: Only a placed order can be cancelled.
`ship` should move a placed order to shipped.

checks.code:
var o = Order.placed
o.ship(trackingNumber: "TR1")
expect(o.summary == "Shipped, tracking TR1")

tests.text: `ship` should leave a delivered order alone.

description.text: Five questions on enums.

questions.question: Why can a `switch` over an enum often leave out `default`?

answers.text: Swift knows every case, so it can check they are all handled
The last case acts as a default
Enums cannot be switched on with `default`

questions.why: Covering every case makes the switch exhaustive, and Swift will tell you when a new case needs handling.

questions.question: What does `Size(rawValue: "XL")` give if there is no such case?
questions.why: Not every raw value matches a case, so this initializer returns an optional.

questions.question: What is the difference between raw values and associated values?

answers.text: Raw values are fixed per case; associated values can differ for every instance

questions.why: `.card(last4: "4242")` carries data chosen when the value is made.

questions.question: What does `CaseIterable` add to an enum?
questions.why: It is perfect for menus and pickers.

questions.question: Why model a screen's loading state as an enum rather than several separate properties?

answers.text: Impossible combinations, like loading and failed at once, cannot exist

questions.why: Each case carries exactly the data that belongs to it, and nothing else.

lessons.title: Protocols

description.text: A **protocol** describes what a type can do, without saying how. It is a list of requirements: properties and methods a type must have.
`{ get }` means the property must be readable. A type **conforms** to the protocol by saying so after its name, and providing everything it asks for:
Now you can write code that works with **anything** describable, without caring what it is:

Protocols are at the heart of Swift. Apple calls Swift a **protocol-oriented** language: instead of building deep class hierarchies, you describe abilities with protocols and give them to any type, struct, enum or class.

items: Define a protocol `Priced` that requires a readable `price: Double`.
Make `Book` and `Coffee` conform to it. `Book` already has a `price`; `Coffee` should work out its price as `2.5` for a small and `3.5` for a large, using a computed property.
Write `totalCost(_:)`, which takes an array of `any Priced` and returns the total price.

checks.code:
let items: [any Priced] = [Book(title: "Dune", price: 12), Coffee(isLarge: true)]
expect(items.count == 2)

tests.text: A large coffee should cost `3.5`, and a small one `2.5`.

checks.code:
let items: [any Priced] = [Book(title: "Dune", price: 12), Coffee(isLarge: false), Coffee(isLarge: true)]
expect(totalCost(items) == 18)

tests.text: `Priced` should be a protocol with a `price` requirement.

lessons.title: Equatable, Hashable and Comparable

description.text: Swift's standard library is built from protocols, and your types can join in. Four you will use constantly:

head: Protocol
What it gives you
rows: Use as a dictionary key or in a set

description.text: For `Equatable` and `Hashable`, you usually just write the name. If all the properties are themselves equatable or hashable, Swift writes the code for you:
`Comparable` needs you to say what "less than" means, with a `static func <`:
`CustomStringConvertible` asks for a `description`:

instructions.text: Make `Card` conform to `Hashable`, `Comparable` and `CustomStringConvertible`:

items: Cards compare by `rank` (a higher rank is greater).
`description` is like `"7♠"`: the rank followed by the suit.

instructions.text: Then create `hand`: the cards in `dealt` with duplicates removed (using a `Set`) and sorted from lowest to highest.

tests.text: Two cards with the same rank and suit should be equal.
A lower rank should be less than a higher one.
`description` should be the rank then the suit.
`hand` should be the unique cards, lowest first.

description.text: An **extension** adds new abilities to a type that already exists, even one you did not write, like `Int` or `String`:
Extensions can add computed properties, methods, initializers and protocol conformances. They cannot add stored properties.
They are also how Swift programmers **organise** code. A common style puts each protocol conformance in its own extension:
And, as you saw in Structs, an `init` written in an extension keeps the free memberwise initializer.

items: Extend `String` with a computed property `isPalindrome`: `true` when the text reads the same backwards, ignoring capital letters. `"Level"` is a palindrome. Use `lowercased()` and `reversed()`.
Extend `Array` where the elements are `Int` with a computed property `average: Double` (`0` for an empty array). Write the extension as `extension Array where Element == Int`.

tests.text: `[2, 4, 9].average` should be `5.0`, and an empty array's average `0`.

description.text: You can extend a **protocol**, too. Anything you add becomes available to every conforming type, for free. This is how a protocol can provide **default behaviour**:
`Robot` wrote nothing but `name`, yet it can `greet()`.
If a protocol **requirement** has a default in an extension, a type can still provide its own version to replace it:

This is the protocol-oriented way to share behaviour: no superclass needed, and it works for structs and enums, not only classes. Much of Swift's own library, such as `map` and `filter` on every collection, comes from protocol extensions.

items: Define a protocol `Shape` that requires `func area() -> Double` and a readable `name: String`.
In a protocol extension, give every `Shape` a method `summary() -> String` that returns `"<name> with area <area>"`, and a default `name` of `"Shape"`.

Make `Square` (with a `side`) and `Circle` (with a `radius`) conform. `Circle` should use the default name; `Square` should have the name `"Square"`. Use `3.0` in place of π to keep the numbers simple.

tests.text: `Circle(radius: 1).summary()` should use the default name: `"Shape with area 3.0"`.
`summary` and the default `name` should come from a protocol extension.

lessons.title: some and any

description.text: When a protocol is used as a type, Swift asks you to say which of two things you mean.
**`some Protocol`** means "one particular type that conforms, which the compiler knows". It is fast and keeps full type information:
**`any Protocol`** means "a box that can hold any conforming type, decided while the program runs". You need it when the actual type can vary, such as an array holding different kinds of things:

description.code: let crowd: [any Greeter] = [Robot(name: "R2"), Person(name: "Ana")]

description.text: The box has a small cost, and some protocols, those with `Self` or associated-type requirements like `Equatable`, have limits on what you can do through it.

The rule of thumb: **write `some` by default; switch to `any` when the type really must vary.** You will see `some` everywhere in SwiftUI, where every view's body is `some View`: a specific view type, built by the compiler, that you never have to spell out.

items: Write `loudest(_:)`, which takes an `[any Animal]` and returns the `name` of the animal whose `sound()` is longest, or `"Nobody"` for an empty array.
Write `echo(_:)`, which takes `some Animal` and returns its sound twice, separated by a space.

instructions.text: `Animal`, `Dog` and `Bird` are written for you.

tests.text: `loudest` should find the longest sound in a mixed array.
You should use `any Animal` and `some Animal`.

description.text: Design a small media library that holds books, films and albums, all described by one protocol.

items: A protocol `Media` requiring `title: String`, `year: Int` and `minutes: Int` (how long it takes to read, watch or listen).
A protocol extension giving every `Media` a `label: String` of `"<title> (<year>)"`.

Three structs conforming to `Media`: `Book` (with `pages`; reading time is 2 minutes a page), `Film` (with `minutes` stored directly) and `Album` (with `tracks: [Int]`, each track's length in minutes; its minutes are the sum).
A function `planWeekend(_ items: [any Media], hours: Int) -> [String]` that picks items in the given order, skipping any that would go over the time available, and returns their labels.

tests.text: A book's minutes should be twice its pages.
An album's minutes should be the sum of its tracks.
`label` should come from the protocol extension.
`planWeekend` should skip items that do not fit, in order.

checks.code:
let items: [any Media] = [Film(title: "A", year: 2000, minutes: 120), Book(title: "B", year: 2001, pages: 300), Album(title: "C", year: 2002, tracks: [30, 30])]
expect(planWeekend(items, hours: 4) == ["A (2000)", "C (2002)"])

description.text: Five questions on protocols and extensions.

questions.question: What does a protocol define?

answers.text: Requirements: what a conforming type must provide
A way to copy a struct
A type that can be created with an initializer

questions.why: A protocol says what, not how; conforming types supply the how.

questions.question: How do you get `==` for a struct whose properties are all `Equatable`?
questions.why: Swift writes the code for you when every property is equatable.

questions.question: What can an extension not add to a type?
questions.why: Extensions can add behaviour, not storage.

questions.question: Where does a protocol's default behaviour come from?
questions.why: Methods in a protocol extension are available to every conforming type.

questions.question: When must you write `any` instead of `some`?

answers.text: When values of different conforming types are mixed, such as in one array

questions.why: `some` is one specific type; `any` is a box that can hold different types.

description.text: Suppose you want a function that swaps the first and last items of an array. You could write one for `[Int]`, another for `[String]`, another for `[Double]`… or write it once, for **any** type:

`<T>` introduces a **type parameter**: a placeholder for a real type, filled in each time the function is called. Inside, `T` stands for "whatever type the caller used", and Swift checks everything is consistent: you cannot sneak a `String` into an `[Int]`.
You have been using generics all along. `Array<Int>` is the long way to write `[Int]`, and `Optional<String>` is `String?`. Swift's collections are written once, generically, and work for every type.
Type parameters can have short names like `T` or `Element`, or descriptive ones when it helps: `func pair<Key, Value>(...)`.

items: Write a generic function `repeated(_:times:)` that takes a value of any type and a count, and returns an array with the value repeated that many times.
Write a generic function `lastTwo(_:)` that returns the last two items of any array, or the whole array if it has fewer than two.

tests.text: You should use a type parameter.

description.text: A plain `T` can be anything, so you can do very little with it: you cannot compare two `T` values, because not every type can be compared. A **constraint** asks for a type that conforms to a protocol, and in return you can use what that protocol provides:
`T: Comparable` says "any type, as long as it is `Comparable`", which is why `>` works.
For more than one requirement, or requirements on related types, use a `where` clause:
And with `some`, which you met in Protocols, there is a lighter way to write a simple constrained parameter:

items: Write `countMatches(_:in:)`, generic over an `Equatable` type, that counts how many times a value appears in an array.
Write `uniqueSorted(_:)`, generic over a type that is both `Hashable` and `Comparable`, that returns the array's unique items, sorted.

tests.text: You should constrain the type parameters.

description.text: Types can be generic too. Here is a **stack**, a pile where you add and remove from the top, that works for any element type:
`private` means only code inside `Stack` can touch `items`, so nobody can mess up the pile. You will learn more about access control later.
You can add abilities only for some element types, with a constrained extension:

Protocols can be generic in their own way, with an **associated type**: a placeholder the conforming type fills in. `Sequence` is like this: its `Element` is whatever it holds. You will use associated types far more often than you write them, so it is enough to recognise one when you see `associatedtype` in a protocol.

instructions.text: Write a generic struct `Queue<Element>`: first in, first out, like a line of people.

items: `mutating func enqueue(_:)` adds to the back.
`mutating func dequeue() -> Element?` removes from the front, or returns `nil` if empty.
`var count: Int`.
Keep the storage `private`.

tests.text: A queue should give items back in the order they were added.

checks.code:
var q = Queue<Int>()
q.enqueue(1); q.enqueue(2); q.enqueue(3)
_ = q.dequeue()
expect(q.count == 2)

tests.text: `Queue` should be generic, with private storage.

description.text: Four questions on generics.

questions.question: In `func first<T>(_ items: [T]) -> T?`, what is `T`?

answers.text: A placeholder for whatever type the caller uses
A type called `T` you must define

questions.why: Each call fills in `T` with a real type.

questions.question: Why does `func biggest<T: Comparable>` allow `>` inside, when `func biggest<T>` does not?

answers.text: It does not: both allow it
The constraint guarantees `T` can be compared
`>` only works on generics with constraints

questions.why: Constraints tell Swift what a type can do.

questions.question: What is `[Int]` the short form of?
questions.why: Arrays are a generic type in Swift's standard library.

questions.question: What does `extension Stack where Element: Numeric` do?

answers.text: Turns every stack into a number
Adds abilities only to stacks of numbers

questions.why: A constrained extension applies only when the condition holds.

description.text: Some operations can fail for reasons you cannot rule out ahead of time: a file is missing, a network request fails, a user types something invalid. An optional says "there might be no value". An **error** says *why* there is none.
An error is any type that conforms to `Error`. Enums are the usual choice, one case per thing that can go wrong:
A function that can fail is marked `throws`, and uses `throw` to report a problem. Throwing ends the function immediately:
Calling a throwing function needs `try`, inside a `do` block, with `catch` blocks to handle the errors:
The final `catch` with no pattern catches everything else, and gives you the error as `error`. The word `try` marks every place that can fail, so you can see the risky lines at a glance.

items: Define an enum `TicketError: Error` with the cases `soldOut` and `tooYoung(minimumAge: Int)`.
Write `buyTicket(age:seatsLeft:) throws -> String`. It throws `soldOut` if `seatsLeft` is `0`, and `tooYoung(minimumAge: 12)` if `age` is under `12`. Otherwise it returns `"Ticket booked"`.
Write `attempt(age:seatsLeft:) -> String`, which calls `buyTicket` and returns its result, `"Sold out"` for `soldOut`, or `"Must be <n> or older"` for `tooYoung`.

tests.text: `attempt(age: 8, seatsLeft: 5)` should be `"Must be 12 or older"`.

description.text: Typed throws
By default a throwing function can throw any `Error`, which is why a final `catch` is needed to be exhaustive. When a function can only throw one error type, you can say so with **typed throws**:
Use typed throws when callers need to handle each case exactly, especially inside a module. For public APIs that may grow new errors, plain `throws` stays more flexible.
try? and try!
`try?` turns a throwing call into an optional: the value if it worked, `nil` if it threw. It is perfect when you do not care *why* something failed:

description.code: let n = try? parse("abc")   // nil

description.text: `try!` says "this cannot fail", and crashes if it does. Like `!` on optionals, keep it for cases where a failure would mean a bug in your own code.
Errors in, errors out

A throwing function can call other throwing functions with plain `try` and let their errors pass straight through to its caller. You do not need `do`/`catch` at every level, only where you can actually handle the problem.

items: Define `enum ScoreError: Error` with `empty` and `outOfRange(Int)`.

Write `parseScore(_:) throws(ScoreError) -> Int` that throws `.empty` for an empty string, `.outOfRange(n)` for a number outside `0...100`, and also `.empty` for text that is not a number. Otherwise it returns the number.
Write `validScores(_:) -> [Int]`, which keeps only the strings that parse, using `try?` and `compactMap`.

description.text: Result
`Result` is an enum that holds either a success value or a failure error:
It is useful when you want to **store** an outcome, or pass it around, rather than handle it right away:
With `async`/`await`, which comes next, you will throw errors far more often than you build `Result` values, but you will meet `Result` in plenty of code.
defer
`defer` schedules code to run when the current scope ends, **however** it ends: a normal finish, a `return`, or a thrown error. It is the place for clean-up you must never forget:

items: Write `safeDivide(_:by:) -> Result<Int, DivisionError>` that returns `.failure(.byZero)` when dividing by zero, and `.success` with the quotient otherwise. `DivisionError` is written for you.
Write `describe(_:)` that takes such a `Result` and returns `"= <n>"` for success or `"Cannot divide by zero"` for failure.
Write `logged(_:) throws -> Int`, which prints `start`, uses `defer` to print `end`, then returns `try safeDivide(...).get()` for `100` divided by its parameter.

tests.text: `describe(safeDivide(1, by: 0))` should be `"Cannot divide by zero"`.
`logged(0)` should throw, but still print `end` after `start`.

description.text: Five questions on errors.

questions.question: What must you write before calling a function marked `throws`?
questions.why: `try` marks each call that can fail.

questions.question: What does `try? riskyThing()` give if it throws?
questions.why: `try?` turns any error into `nil`.

questions.question: What does `throws(ParseError)` add over plain `throws`?

answers.text: Callers know exactly which error type can be thrown, so they can switch over it completely
It means the function never throws

questions.why: That is typed throws.

questions.question: When does a `defer` block run?

answers.text: Only if an error is thrown
When the scope ends, whether normally, by returning, or by throwing

questions.why: It is for clean-up that must always happen.

questions.question: Which is the best fit for a missing middle name: an optional or an error?

answers.text: An optional: nothing went wrong, there is just no value

questions.why: Errors explain failures; optionals represent values that may simply be absent.

lessons.title: Project: a library system

description.text: This is the project for the Modelling with types chapter. It uses structs, classes, enums, protocols and errors together, the way a real program does.

You are building the core of a lending library: the members, the books, and the rules for borrowing and returning. There is no step-by-step guide. Plan it on paper first: which things are values, which thing is shared, and what can go wrong?
When every test passes, you have a solid foundation in modelling with Swift's types.

instructions.text: **User stories**

items: A `Book` struct has an `isbn` (`String`), a `title` (`String`) and an `author` (`String`). Books are `Hashable`.
A `Member` struct has an `id` (`Int`), a `name` (`String`) and a `tier`, an enum `Tier` with the cases `standard` and `premium`.
`Tier` has a computed property `loanLimit`: `3` for standard members and `10` for premium.
An enum `LibraryError: Error` has the cases `unknownBook`, `unknownMember`, `alreadyOnLoan`, `notOnLoan` and `limitReached(limit: Int)`.
A `final class Library` holds the catalogue and the loans. It has:
`func add(_ book: Book)` and `func register(_ member: Member)`,
`func lend(isbn: String, to memberID: Int) throws(LibraryError)`, which throws the right error for an unknown book or member, a book already on loan, or a member at their limit,
`func giveBack(isbn: String) throws(LibraryError)`, which throws `notOnLoan` if the book was not on loan (or `unknownBook` if the library does not have it),
`func books(on memberID: Int) -> [Book]`: the books a member has, sorted by title,
`var available: [Book]`: every book not on loan, sorted by title.
Lending and returning must keep the library consistent: a book is on loan to at most one member at a time.

lessons.seed: // Plan first: which things are values, which is shared, and what can go wrong?

tests.text: Premium members should be able to borrow 10 books, and standard members 3.
Lending should move a book from `available` to the member's books.
Lending an unknown book or to an unknown member should throw the right error.
A book on loan should not be lent again.
A standard member should be stopped at 3 books, with the limit in the error.
Returning a book should make it available again, and returning it twice should throw `notOnLoan`.
`lend` and `giveBack` should use typed throws, and `Library` should be a final class.

hints: A dictionary from ISBN to member ID is a simple way to record loans. It makes "on loan to at most one member" true by construction.
Count a member's loans with `loans.values.filter { $0 == memberID }.count`.

chapters.title: Modern Swift
chapters.summary: Concurrency, Codable, testing and what is new in Swift 6.4.

description.text: Some work takes time: downloading a file, reading from a disk, asking a server. An app must not freeze while it waits. Swift's answer is **async functions**.
Mark a function `async` when it may need to wait. Call it with `await`, which marks the spot where your code may pause:

While one piece of code is paused at an `await`, the system is free to do other work, such as keeping your app's interface responsive. When the result arrives, your code carries on from the same line, with all its variables just as they were. It reads top to bottom, like ordinary code, which is the whole point.
`async` combines with `throws`. Write both on the function, and both on the call, in this order:

description.code:
func download(_ name: String) async throws -> String { ... }
let file = try await download("photo.jpg")

description.text: You can only `await` inside something that is itself async. In an app, you start async work from ordinary code with `Task`:
Here, the code you write runs at the top level of a program, which Swift allows to `await` directly.

items: Write `fetchUsername(id:) async -> String` that waits `10` milliseconds with `try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(10))`, then returns `"user\(id)"`.
Write `fetchGreeting(id:) async -> String` that awaits `fetchUsername` and returns `"Welcome back, <name>!"`.
Print `await fetchGreeting(id: 42)`.

checks.code:
let greeting = await fetchGreeting(id: 7)
expect(greeting == "Welcome back, user7!")

tests.text: Your program should print `Welcome back, user42!`.
Both functions should be `async`, and `fetchUsername` should sleep.

lessons.title: Doing things at the same time

description.text: `await` one thing after another, and each waits for the one before:

description.code:
let a = await fetchPrice("apples")   // 1 second
let b = await fetchPrice("pears")    // another second

description.text: If the two do not depend on each other, start them **together** with `async let`. Each begins straight away, and you `await` the results when you need them:

description.code:
async let a = fetchPrice("apples")
async let b = fetchPrice("pears")
let total = await a + b              // about 1 second in all

description.text: When you have a list of things to do in parallel, and do not know how many ahead of time, use a **task group**:

`async let` and task groups are **structured concurrency**: the child tasks cannot outlive the code that started them. If the parent finishes, throws or is cancelled, Swift waits for or cancels the children. Nothing is left running in the background by accident.

instructions.text: `fetchPrice(_:)` is written for you; it waits a little and returns a price.

items: Write `basket() async -> Double`, which fetches `"apples"` and `"pears"` **at the same time** with `async let` and returns their sum.
Write `totalPrice(of:) async -> Double`, which fetches the price of every item in an array in parallel with a task group and returns the sum.

description.text: When several tasks run at once, they must not change the same data at the same moment. If two tasks both read a counter as 5 and both write 6, one increment is lost. This is a **data race**, and it causes the worst kind of bug: rare, random and hard to reproduce.
An **actor** is a type that protects its state from data races. It looks like a class, but only one task can be inside it at a time:
From outside, every use of an actor is `await`ed, because you may have to wait your turn:
Inside the actor, its own methods use its state directly, with no `await`, because they already have exclusive access.
`private(set)` means anyone may read `balance`, but only the actor itself can change it.

Swift 6 checks for data races **when it compiles**. If your code could race, it will not build. That can feel strict at first, but it means a whole category of crashes simply cannot reach the people using your app.

instructions.text: Write an actor `TicketCounter`:

items: `private(set) var sold = 0` and a constant `capacity`, set by `init(capacity:)`.
`func sell() -> Bool`: if there is room, add one to `sold` and return `true`; otherwise return `false`.

instructions.text: The code at the bottom sells tickets from 100 tasks at once. With an actor, exactly `capacity` tickets are sold, never more.

tests.text: Selling from many tasks at once should never sell more than the capacity.
`sell()` should return `false` once the counter is full.

lessons.title: The main actor and Sendable

description.text: The main actor
Every app has one special actor: the **main actor**. It runs your user interface. All drawing and every update to what is on screen happens there.

Since Xcode 26, a new app project puts your code on the main actor **by default**. It is called "approachable concurrency", and the exercises on this site use the same settings. It means everyday code needs no annotations at all: it simply runs on the main actor, safe to touch the interface.
When you have slow work that should **not** hold up the interface, such as resizing a big image or parsing a large file, mark it `@concurrent`. It then runs in the background, and callers `await` it:
`nonisolated` marks something that belongs to no actor at all, such as a pure function that only uses its parameters.
Sendable
Values that cross from one actor or task to another must be safe to share. Swift calls these types **Sendable**:

items: Structs and enums made of sendable parts are sendable automatically.
Actors are always sendable: they protect themselves.
A class is only sendable if it is `final` with constant (`let`) sendable properties, or protects its state some other way.

description.text: When the compiler says a type "is not Sendable", it has found a place where data could be raced. The usual fixes, in order: make it a struct, make it an actor, or keep it on one actor (often the main actor) and do not send it anywhere.

items: Write `nonisolated func wordCount(_ text: String) -> Int` that counts the words in `text`, splitting on spaces.
Write `@concurrent func countAll(_ texts: [String]) async -> Int` that adds up `wordCount` for every text.
Make `Article` a struct with `title` and `body`, so it is `Sendable`, and `print(await countAll(articles.map(\.body)))`.

lessons.seed:
let articles = [
    Article(title: "Swift", body: "Swift is fast"),
    Article(title: "Apps", body: "Apps are fun"),
]

tests.text: `countAll` should add up every text, off the main actor.

checks.code:
let n = await countAll(["a b", "c d e"])
expect(n == 5)

tests.text: `Article` should be a struct, and the program should print `6`.

description.text: Async sequences
Some data arrives over time: messages in a chat, readings from a sensor, lines of a file being downloaded. An **async sequence** delivers values one at a time, and you loop over it with `for await`:
You can make your own with `AsyncStream`. Its closure gets a **continuation**: call `yield` to send a value, and `finish` when there are no more:
Cancellation

A task can be **cancelled**, for example when the person leaves the screen that started it. Cancellation does not stop code by force; it sets a flag, and well-behaved async code checks it and stops early:
`Task.sleep` notices cancellation too, and throws. In SwiftUI, the `.task` modifier starts work when a view appears and cancels it automatically when the view goes away.

items: Write `ticks(_ count: Int) -> AsyncStream<Int>`, which yields `1` up to `count`, then finishes.
Write `sumTicks(_:) async -> Int`, which loops over `ticks` with `for await` and returns the sum.

Write `sumUntilCancelled() async -> Int`, which adds up `1, 2, 3, …` forever, but checks `Task.isCancelled` on every pass and returns the sum so far when cancelled. Sleep for `1` millisecond on every pass with `try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(1))`.

tests.text: `sumUntilCancelled` should stop when its task is cancelled.
You should use `for await` and check for cancellation.

description.text: Six questions on Swift concurrency.

questions.question: What does `await` mark?

answers.text: A line that runs in the background
A place where the code may pause while it waits, letting other work run

questions.why: The function pauses there and resumes on the same line when the result is ready.

questions.question: Two independent downloads take a second each. What is the fastest way to get both?

answers.text: Start both with `async let`, then `await` both

questions.why: `async let` starts each immediately, so they overlap.

questions.question: What problem do actors solve?

answers.text: Data races: two tasks changing the same state at once

questions.why: Only one task can be inside an actor at a time.

questions.question: In a new Xcode 27 app project, where does your code run unless it says otherwise?
questions.why: Approachable concurrency makes the main actor the default.

questions.question: What does marking a function `@concurrent` do?

answers.text: Runs it off the main actor, so heavy work does not hold up the interface

questions.why: Use it for slow work, and `await` it from the main actor.

questions.question: What happens when you cancel a task?

answers.text: A flag is set; well-behaved code checks it and stops early

questions.why: Cancellation is cooperative: check `Task.isCancelled` or call `Task.checkCancellation()`.

description.text: Apps constantly turn their data into text and back: to save it to a file, or to send it to and from a server. The most common format is **JSON**:

description.code: { "title": "Dune", "pages": 412, "isFavourite": true }

description.text: Swift does nearly all the work for you through the `Codable` protocol. Mark a type `Codable`, and as long as its properties are codable too (strings, numbers, Bools, arrays, dictionaries, optionals and other codable types), Swift writes the conversion code itself:
**Decoding** turns JSON into your type. JSON arrives as `Data`, raw bytes; `Data(text.utf8)` makes some from a string:
`#"..."#` is a **raw string**: inside it, quotes and backslashes are just characters, which makes JSON easy to write.
**Encoding** goes the other way:
Decoding throws if the JSON does not match your type: a missing key, a string where a number should be. That is a feature: bad data is caught at the edge of your app, not deep inside it.

items: Make `Recipe` a `Codable` struct with `name` (`String`), `minutes` (`Int`) and `ingredients` (`[String]`).
Decode `json` into a constant `recipe`.
Create `encoded`: `recipe` encoded back to a JSON `String` with sorted keys.

tests.text: `recipe` should be decoded from the JSON.
`encoded` should be the JSON with sorted keys.

description.text: Real JSON rarely uses Swift's naming style. Servers often write keys in `snake_case`, like `"release_year"`. Two tools bridge the gap.
The decoder can convert snake_case for you:

description.code:
let decoder = JSONDecoder()
decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase   // release_year -> releaseYear

description.text: For anything else, list the keys yourself with a nested `CodingKeys` enum. Each case is a property name; its raw value is the key in the JSON:
Nested JSON maps to nested types, and keys that might be missing map to optionals:
A good habit: write your Swift types the way your *app* wants them, then use `CodingKeys` and strategies to fit the JSON to them, rather than letting a server's naming leak through your code.

instructions.text: Decode `json` into `Show`:

items: `Show` has `title`, `firstAired` (from `"first_aired"`), `seasons` (an array of `Season`) and an optional `network`.
`Season` has `number` and `episodeCount`, where `episodeCount` comes from the key `"episodes"`.
Use `.convertFromSnakeCase` for `first_aired`, and a `CodingKeys` enum in `Season`.
Create `show` by decoding, and `totalEpisodes`: the total across all seasons.

tests.text: `show.title` should be `"Planet Swift"` and `show.firstAired` should be `2019`.

description.text: A weather service sends a forecast as JSON. Decode it, and turn it into a short report a person would want to read.

items: Model the JSON with `Codable` types. Use `.convertFromSnakeCase`.
Write `report(from json: String) throws -> String` that decodes the forecast and returns lines like this, one per day, joined with new lines:

instructions.code:
Mon: 18° to 24°, rain likely
Tue: 15° to 20°

instructions.text: A day says `, rain likely` when its `rain_chance` is `0.5` or more. Temperatures are whole numbers.

items: If the JSON cannot be decoded, `report` should throw.

tests.text: The report for the sample forecast should list both days.

checks.code:
let text = try? report(from: sample)
expect(text == "Mon: 18° to 24°, rain likely\nTue: 15° to 20°")

description.text: Four questions on Codable and JSON.

questions.question: What do you need to write for Swift to encode and decode a struct of strings and numbers?
questions.why: Swift writes the code when every property is codable.

questions.question: The JSON key is `"user_name"` and your property is `userName`. What is the simplest fix?
questions.why: The strategy converts snake_case keys for the whole decode.

questions.question: A key is sometimes missing from the JSON. How should the property be declared?
questions.why: Missing or null keys decode to `nil` for optional properties.

questions.question: What happens when JSON does not match your type?
questions.why: Bad data is caught where it enters your app.

description.text: Every lesson on this site has been checked by tests: small pieces of code that run your code and check the answer. You have been on the receiving end of testing all along. Now you will write your own.

A test is code that says: "given this input, I expect that output." Once written, it checks your work in a second, forever. Tests let you change code without fear: if you break something, a test tells you straight away, long before anyone using your app finds out.
Swift has a modern testing library called **Swift Testing**. A test is a function marked `@Test`, and `#expect` checks a condition:
When an expectation fails, Swift Testing shows you the values on both sides, so you can see at a glance what went wrong:

description.code: Expectation failed: (price → 118.0) == 120

description.text: Tests live in their own **test target**, separate from your app, so they never ship to the people using it. The next lessons happen on your Mac, in Terminal and Xcode.

blocks.text: You may also meet **XCTest**, Apple's older testing framework, in existing projects. As of Swift 6.4 the two work together, so a project can move to Swift Testing one file at a time.

questions.question: What does `#expect(total == 10)` do?

description.text: Swift 6.4 arrived in September 2026 with Xcode 27. This module covers the changes you are most likely to use. Everything you have learned so far already uses Swift 6.4.

The first is small but saves a lot of typing. A struct's free memberwise initializer has a parameter for each stored property. Before Swift 6.4, a single `private` property, even one with a default value, made the whole initializer `private`, so nobody outside the struct could use it.
Now, `private` stored properties **with a default value** are simply left out of the memberwise initializer, and it stays usable:
This makes it easy to keep bookkeeping details private without writing an initializer by hand.

weak let

A `weak` reference used to have to be a `var`, because Swift sets it to `nil` when its object goes away. That made a class containing one hard to mark `Sendable`. Swift 6.4 allows `weak let`: a weak reference you cannot reassign yourself, which Swift can still clear. A `final class` with only `let` properties, including `weak let`, can be `Sendable`:

description.text: anyAppleOS

Apple's platforms now share one version number: iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, tvOS 27 and visionOS 27. Swift 6.4 lets you say "this needs the 2026 releases or later, on any Apple platform" in one go:

@diagnose

Sometimes you knowingly use something deprecated while you move away from it, and the warnings drown out the ones that matter. Swift 6.4's `@diagnose` changes how a single declaration's warnings are reported, without affecting the rest of your code:

description.text: **SwiftUI** is Apple's way of building interfaces for every Apple platform. Instead of writing step-by-step instructions ("make a label, put it here, change its text when…"), you **describe** what the screen should look like for the current data, and SwiftUI keeps the screen matching that description as the data changes.
A screen is made of **views**. A view is a struct that conforms to `View` and has one requirement, a `body`:

You recognise all of this now: a struct, a protocol, a computed property, and `some View`, which means "a specific view type the compiler works out". Views are small, cheap values. SwiftUI makes and throws them away constantly; that is normal.
Every app starts at a struct marked `@main` that conforms to `App`. Its `body` holds **scenes**, such as a window:
Open your **Hello** project from the last chapter: `HelloApp.swift` and `ContentView.swift` look just like this.
Previews
At the bottom of `ContentView.swift` is a **preview**:

The canvas (⌥⌘↩) shows it live and updates as you type. You can have several previews in a file, each showing a different state. In Xcode 27, iPhone previews have **resize handles**, because iPhone apps can now be resized on iOS 27: drag them to check your layout at different sizes.

description.text: Text
`Text` shows read-only text. Style it with **modifiers**, methods that return a changed copy of the view:

    .fontWeight(.bold)
    .foregroundStyle(.blue)

description.text: Use the built-in text styles (`.largeTitle`, `.title`, `.headline`, `.body`, `.caption` and so on) rather than fixed sizes. They grow and shrink with the reader's preferred text size, a setting many people rely on.

`Image("photo")` shows an image you have added to your project's **Assets** catalogue. `Image(systemName:)` shows one of the thousands of **SF Symbols**: icons designed by Apple to match the system font, in every weight and size:

        .font(.title)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text("Freely Given")
            .font(.headline)
        Text("Asteria Technology")
            .font(.subheadline)

        .monospacedDigit()

description.text: `Spacer()` takes up all the spare room, pushing its neighbours apart. `alignment:` lines children up along the stack's edge, and `spacing:` sets the gap between them.
How SwiftUI sizes things

items: A parent offers its child some space.
The child decides its own size: text takes what it needs, shapes and spacers take everything offered.
The parent places the child.

description.text: So `.frame(width: 200)` does not stretch a `Text`; it offers 200 points and centres the text inside. `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` asks for all the width available, which is how you make a full-width button.

lessons.title: @State

description.text: Views are structs, and a view's `body` is recomputed often, so ordinary properties cannot hold anything that changes. When a view needs its own changing value, mark the property `@State`:
When `count` changes, SwiftUI notices, recomputes `body`, and updates only what changed on screen. You never redraw anything yourself.
Rules of thumb:

items: Make `@State` properties `private`. They belong to this view alone.
Give them a starting value where they are declared. In Xcode 27, `@State` is a macro, and it reports an error if you also set a different value in `init`.
Keep state as small as possible, and derive everything else. If you can compute a value from other state, make it a computed property, not more state.

blocks.text: In iOS 27 and macOS 27, `@State` creates its value once per view lifetime, even when the parent view is recreated. This matters when the value is an object, as you will see shortly.

lessons.title: Bindings and controls

description.text: Controls like text fields and toggles both **show** a value and **change** it. They need a two-way connection to your state, called a **binding**. Put `$` in front of a state property to get its binding:
`name` is the value; `$name` is a binding to it. The text field reads through the binding to show the text and writes through it as you type.
`Form` arranges controls the way Settings does, and adapts to each platform.
Passing a binding down
When a child view should change its parent's state, give it a `@Binding` property. The child does not own the value; it borrows the parent's:
This is the heart of SwiftUI data flow: **one source of truth**. Each value is owned in exactly one place, with `@State`, and everything else reads it or binds to it.

description.text: Apps feel at home when they use the system's building blocks. Three habits get you most of the way.

lessons.title: App Intents, Siri and Shortcuts

description.text: **App Intents** describe the things your app can do, so the rest of the system can do them too: Siri, the Shortcuts app, Spotlight, the Action button, widgets and controls. In iOS 27, App Intents is *the* way apps work with Siri; the older SiriKit is being retired.
An intent is a struct with a title and a `perform` method:
`@Parameter` marks an input the system can ask for. To make it available the moment your app is installed, with phrases people can say, add an **app shortcut**:
Every phrase must include the app's name. Now "Hey Siri, log a habit in Habits" works, and the action appears in Shortcuts and Spotlight.

Intents run their code in your app's process, often without showing any interface, so keep your model logic separate from your views. That is one more reason the course has asked you to keep logic in the model.

description.text: Widgets put a glance of your app on the Home Screen, Lock Screen, Mac desktop, in StandBy and on Apple Watch. They are SwiftUI views, but they do not run all the time: the system asks your widget for a **timeline** of entries, and shows each at its time.
Add one with **File › New › Target › Widget Extension**. The template gives you three parts.
An **entry**: the data for one moment.
A **provider**: makes entries.
And the **widget**: its view and configuration.

The widget is a separate process, so it cannot read your app's memory. Share data through an **App Group**: add the App Groups capability to both targets, then point SwiftData or `UserDefaults(suiteName:)` at the group. When the app changes the data, call `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadAllTimelines()`. Buttons in widgets run App Intents, so a widget can log a habit without opening the app.

description.text: CloudKit has a few rules for models, because data from two devices must merge:

items: Every property needs a default value or must be optional.
Relationships must be optional.
Unique constraints (`@Attribute(.unique)`) are not allowed.

description.text: So `var name: String = ""` and `var habit: Habit?`, not `var name: String` with no default.

answers.text: Records arrive from other devices piece by piece, so every property must have a value it can start with

description.text: If your app has accounts, **Sign in with Apple** gives people a private, one-tap way to sign in. They can hide their real email address behind a relay address, and the App Store requires it as an option whenever you offer other third-party sign-in services.

lessons.title: Windows and scenes on the Mac

description.text: The SwiftUI you know runs on the Mac. What makes an app feel truly at home there is how it uses **windows**, **menus** and the **keyboard**. You describe these with **scenes** in your `App`:

items: **`WindowGroup`** can open many windows of the same kind: ⌘N makes another.
**`Window`** is a single, unique window. Open it from code with `@Environment(\.openWindow)`, then `openWindow(id: "stats")`.
**`Settings`** gives your app a proper **Settings…** item in the app menu, with ⌘, as its shortcut.
**`MenuBarExtra`** adds an item to the menu bar at the top of the screen. With `.menuBarExtraStyle(.window)` it opens a small window of SwiftUI.

description.text: To add a Mac version of an existing iOS app, select your project, choose the target, and add **Mac** under **Supported Destinations**. Then adapt where the Mac deserves something better: sidebars, menus, keyboard shortcuts, pointer hover.

It has a Settings scene, opened with ⌘,.
It has a menu bar extra.

questions.why: The `Settings` scene is built for app preferences.

lessons.title: Menus and keyboard shortcuts

description.text: Mac users live on the keyboard and the menu bar. Every important action should be in a menu, and the common ones should have shortcuts.
Add commands to the menu bar with `.commands` on a scene:
`CommandMenu` adds a whole new menu; `CommandGroup` adds items to an existing one, such as after **File › New**.
Keyboard shortcuts work on views too, including buttons in toolbars: `.keyboardShortcut(.defaultAction)` makes a button respond to Return.
The menu bar also shows minimal icons beside items by default on macOS 27. If an item deserves its icon, give its label `.labelStyle(.titleAndIcon)`.
Look at a polished Mac app you love, open each menu, and notice how much lives there. Your app should feel the same.

checklist: My app has a Note menu with three commands and shortcuts.
An Import… item appears in the File menu after New.

questions.question: What is the difference between `CommandMenu` and `CommandGroup`?

answers.text: `CommandMenu` adds a new menu; `CommandGroup` adds items to an existing menu

questions.why: Use the system's menus where they fit, and your own where they do not.

lessons.title: Document-based apps

description.text: Some apps are about **documents**: files people create, name, save anywhere, and open again. SwiftUI's `DocumentGroup` gives you the whole system experience: open and save panels, recent documents, duplicate, rename, versions, and iCloud Drive.
With SwiftData, a document app is a short step from what you know:

`contentType` is a **uniform type identifier**: the type of file your app owns. You declare it in your target's **Info › Exported Type Identifiers**, with a file extension such as `.sketchbook`, and in code:

New in iOS 27 and macOS 27, document apps can offer several ways to start a document, from a blank page or from a photo for example, with `DocumentCreationSource` and `NewDocumentButton` in a document launch scene. And documents that are not SwiftData can separate the model from writing to disk with `WritableDocument`, so saving happens off the main actor while you keep typing.

checklist: My app declares its own document type with a file extension.
I can create, save, close and reopen a document, and see it in Recent documents.

questions.question: What does `DocumentGroup` give you for free?

answers.text: Open and save panels, recent documents, renaming, versions and iCloud Drive

questions.why: The system document experience comes with the scene.

description.text: When SwiftUI is not enough
SwiftUI covers most needs, but the Mac's older framework, **AppKit**, still has views SwiftUI lacks. Wrap one with `NSViewRepresentable`:
`make` creates the AppKit view once; `update` pushes SwiftUI's state into it; the **coordinator** carries changes back. On iOS, `UIViewRepresentable` does the same for UIKit.
The App Sandbox

Mac apps from the App Store run in the **App Sandbox**: they can only reach their own container unless they ask. Under **Signing & Capabilities › App Sandbox**, tick what your app needs: outgoing network connections, files the user selects, the camera, and so on. Files a person chooses in an open panel are always allowed, which is why document apps work naturally in the sandbox.
Ask for as little as you can. App Review checks that each entitlement is needed.

questions.question: In `NSViewRepresentable`, what does `updateNSView` do?

answers.text: Pushes the current SwiftUI state into the AppKit view whenever it changes

questions.why: Make once; update many times.

questions.why: The sandbox blocks network access unless you ask for it.

lessons.title: Testing your app's logic

description.text: You wrote tests for a package in Modern Swift. Apps test the same way. A new project made with the **Swift Testing** option already has a test target; otherwise add one with **File › New › Target › Unit Testing Bundle**.
Test the parts that hold your app's rules, not its views:

Notice that the function takes the calendar and the end date as parameters, instead of reading `Date.now`. Code that depends on "now" is hard to test; code that is *given* the date is easy. Designing for testability usually makes code better anyway.
For SwiftData models, create an in-memory container in the test, so each test starts from nothing:

description.code:
let container = try ModelContainer(for: Habit.self, configurations: ModelConfiguration(isStoredInMemoryOnly: true))
let context = ModelContext(container)

checklist: My Habits app's streak logic has at least five Swift Testing tests.
The streak functions take the date and calendar as parameters.
⌘U runs every test, and they pass.

questions.question: Why pass the date into a function rather than reading `Date.now` inside it?

answers.text: Tests can choose the date, so the result is predictable

questions.why: Code that is given its inputs is easy to test.

lessons.title: UI tests and accessibility audits

description.text: **UI tests** drive your real app the way a person would: tapping, typing, swiping, and checking what appears. They use the XCTest framework's `XCUIApplication`:
Elements are found by their labels, the same labels VoiceOver reads, so a well-labelled app is also an easy app to test.
`performAccessibilityAudit()` checks the current screen for common problems: missing labels, text that does not scale, poor contrast, and controls too small to tap. Run it on each important screen.
UI tests are slower than unit tests, so keep them for your app's most important journeys, and test logic with unit tests.

blocks.text: Click the record button at the bottom of the editor while a UI test function is selected, use your app, and Xcode writes the test code for you. Tidy it up afterwards.

lessons.title: Debugging

description.text: Every programmer spends much of their time finding out why something does not work. Xcode gives you good tools for it.

**Breakpoints.** Click a line number in the editor to add a breakpoint. When the running app reaches that line, it pauses, and the debug area shows every variable's value. Step over a line with F6, step into a function with F7, and continue with ⌃⌘Y.
**The console.** While paused, type commands at the `(lldb)` prompt:

description.code:
p habit.name
po habits.count

description.text: `p` prints a value; `po` prints an object's description. You can even change values, `expression streak = 10`, to try a theory without rebuilding.
**Conditional breakpoints.** Right-click a breakpoint, choose **Edit Breakpoint**, and add a condition like `habit.name == "Read"` so it only stops when it matters.
**The view debugger.** Click **Debug View Hierarchy** in the debug bar to see your interface exploded into 3D layers. It shows why a view is hidden, clipped, or the wrong size.
**Logging.** `print` is fine for a quick look. For logs you keep, use `Logger` from the `os` framework, which is fast, has levels, and keeps private data private:

description.code:
import os

let log = Logger(subsystem: "com.yourname.Habits", category: "sync")
log.info("Synced \(count) habits")
log.error("Sync failed: \(error.localizedDescription, privacy: .public)")

description.text: The best debugging habit is not a tool: change one thing at a time, and check what happened.

I printed a value with `p` at the LLDB prompt.
I used the view debugger to inspect a screen.
My app logs with `Logger` instead of `print`.

answers.text: Pauses the running app at that line, so you can inspect its state

questions.why: You see exactly what your code sees.

lessons.title: Performance with Instruments

description.text: When an app stutters, drains the battery or starts slowly, **Instruments** shows you why. Choose **Product › Profile** (⌘I) to build for profiling and open it.
Templates worth knowing:

head: Template
Finds
rows: Where the CPU spends its time
Views whose bodies run too often or too slowly
Moments the main actor was blocked and the app froze

description.text: Record while you use the slow part of your app, then stop and select the slow stretch of the timeline. In Instruments 27, **Top Functions** lists where the time went in just that stretch, and Quick Open (⇧⌘O) jumps straight to the function in your code.
The usual SwiftUI fixes:

items: Move heavy work out of `body`: compute it once in the model, not on every redraw.
Mark genuinely slow work `@concurrent`, so it runs off the main actor.
Use `LazyVStack` or `List` for long lists, so only visible rows are made.
Keep `@Observable` models granular, so a change only redraws the views that read it.

description.text: Then profile again, to check the fix worked. Xcode 27's Organizer shows the same kinds of problems from real users' devices once your app ships, with **Metric Goals** for launch time, hangs, hitches, battery and storage.

checklist: I profiled my app with the Time Profiler and found its busiest function.
I checked a long list with the SwiftUI instrument.
I profiled again after a change, to confirm it helped.

questions.question: Your app freezes for a moment when a screen opens. Which instrument shows why?
questions.why: A freeze is the main actor being blocked.

lessons.title: Speaking every language

description.text: Apple's platforms are used in nearly every country. Supporting more languages is one of the best ways to reach more people, and Xcode makes it straightforward.

SwiftUI text written as literals, like `Text("Today")`, is **localizable** already. Add a **String Catalog** with **File › New › File › String Catalog**, and when you build, Xcode collects every string from your code into it.

In Xcode 27 you can let the coding assistant prepare your project: it finds strings, sets up the catalog, and translates. In the String Catalog, the **Generate Translations** button adds a language for you. Treat machine translations as a draft: have a native speaker review them, and run the app in each language to check nothing is cut off.
Plurals are handled per language, which matters because languages count differently:

description.code: Text("\(count) habits")   // the catalog lets you vary this for 1, 2, few, many…

description.text: Format numbers, dates and currencies with Swift's formatters, so they follow each region's conventions:

description.code:
Text(price, format: .currency(code: "EUR"))
Text(date, format: .dateTime.day().month(.wide))

description.text: To try a language, edit your scheme's **Run › Options › App Language**, or set it in Device Hub.

answers.text: Formatters follow each region's conventions for symbols, spacing and separators
The euro sign is not allowed

lessons.title: App Store Connect

description.text: This chapter takes an app from your Mac to the world. It needs the **Apple Developer Program** membership from here on.

**App Store Connect** ([appstoreconnect.apple.com](https://appstoreconnect.apple.com), and an app of the same name) is where you manage everything about your apps after Xcode: their store pages, builds, testers, prices, sales, ratings and reviews.
Before your first app

items: **Agreements, Tax and Banking.** Accept the Free Apps agreement to publish free apps. To sell apps or in-app purchases, also complete the Paid Apps agreement, with your bank and tax details.
**Users and Access.** Invite people who help you, with roles that limit what they can change.

description.text: Create the app record
Choose **Apps › +  › New App**, then give:

items: the **platforms**,
the **name** people see on the store (it must be unique on the store, and can differ from the name under the icon),
the **primary language**,
the **bundle ID**, which must match your Xcode target exactly,
a **SKU**, any private reference of yours, like `HABITS1`.

description.text: Versions and builds
Two numbers identify every upload, both set on your target's **General** tab:

items: **Version** (`1.0`, `1.1`, `2.0`) is what people see on the store.
**Build** (`1`, `2`, `3`…) must increase with every upload, even for the same version.
