lessons.title: TestFlight

description.text: Before release, let real people try your app. **TestFlight** delivers test builds to testers' devices through Apple's TestFlight app.
Upload a build

items: Choose **Any iOS Device** as the run destination.
Choose **Product › Archive**. Xcode builds a release version and opens the **Organizer**.
Select the archive and click **Distribute App**, then **App Store Connect**. Xcode signs it and uploads it.

description.text: After a few minutes of processing, the build appears in App Store Connect's **TestFlight** tab.
Testers

items: **Internal testers**: up to 100 members of your team in App Store Connect. They can test a build as soon as it has processed.
**External testers**: up to 10,000 people, invited by email or with a **public link**. The first build of each version goes through a short **beta review** first.

description.text: Add **What to Test** notes so testers know what to look at. Testers send feedback with screenshots straight from the TestFlight app, and crash reports arrive in Xcode's Organizer.
Builds expire after 90 days, so testers always have something recent.
Xcode Cloud

Uploading by hand gets old quickly. **Xcode Cloud** builds, tests and delivers your app on Apple's servers whenever you push to your Git repository. In Xcode 27, its setup connects your project to your repository and starts a first build in a few steps (**Integrate › Create Workflow**). A workflow can run your tests on every change and send each successful build to TestFlight automatically. Membership includes a monthly allowance of compute hours.

answers.text: Internal testers on your App Store Connect team

description.text: Every app on the App Store is reviewed by people at Apple against the **App Review Guidelines**. Read them once, before you design anything big: they are clear, and most rejections come from not having read them. The most common issues:

items: **Crashes and broken features.** Test the exact build you submit, on a real device.
**Placeholder content**, or a demo that needs a login reviewers do not have. Give them a demo account in the review notes.
**Incomplete information**: a missing privacy policy link, or screenshots that do not show the app.
**Account deletion.** If people can create an account in your app, they must be able to delete it in your app.
**Payments.** Digital goods sold in the app must use in-app purchase.

description.text: Privacy
Apple takes privacy seriously, and so should you.

items: **Privacy nutrition labels.** In App Store Connect you declare what data your app collects, how it is used, and whether it tracks people. Be accurate: it is shown on your store page.

**The privacy manifest.** A file named `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` in your project declares the data you collect and your reasons for using certain system APIs (such as reading a file's timestamp). Third-party libraries ship their own.
**Permission prompts.** Each request (camera, location, photos, contacts) needs a usage description in your target's Info settings, explaining in plain words why you need it.
**Tracking.** Following people across other companies' apps and websites requires asking with App Tracking Transparency. The best answer is not to track at all.

description.text: The simplest privacy policy is the one where your app collects nothing, and many good apps can.

questions.question: Your app lets people create accounts. What must it also offer?

answers.text: Sign in with a phone number
A way to delete the account from inside the app

answers.text: The privacy manifest: the data your app collects and why it uses certain APIs

lessons.title: Releasing your app

description.text: The store page
In App Store Connect, prepare the version for submission:

items: **Screenshots** for the device sizes your app supports (the current largest iPhone size is required; smaller sizes can reuse it). Show the real app, doing its best thing.
A **description**, **keywords**, a **subtitle**, and a **support URL**.
An **age rating**, by answering a short questionnaire.
The **build** to release, picked from your TestFlight builds.

description.text: Then **Add for Review** and **Submit**. Most apps are reviewed within a day or two. You can release automatically when approved, or by hand, or on a date, and you can phase a release out to a growing share of users over a week.
Mac apps outside the App Store
On the Mac you may also distribute an app yourself, from your own website. macOS trusts it if it is:

items: **Signed** with your **Developer ID Application** certificate (Xcode creates it for you),
built with the **Hardened Runtime** capability, and
**notarized**: scanned by Apple's notary service, which takes a few minutes.

description.text: In the Organizer, choose **Distribute App › Direct Distribution**: Xcode signs, uploads for notarization, and gives you a notarized app to put in a disk image or zip.
After launch

Xcode's **Organizer** shows crashes, hangs, energy use, storage and launch time from real devices, against Xcode 27's **Metric Goals**. Read reviews and reply to them in App Store Connect. Fix what hurts most, ship small updates often, and keep the build number going up.

description.text: You have reached the last module. Its project is the real test of everything you have learned: an app of **your own**, designed by you, shipped to real people.
Choose well

The best first app solves a small problem you actually have. You will use it every day, so you will notice what is wrong with it, and you will finish it because you want it to exist. Some shapes that work well:

items: a tool for a hobby (a climbing log, a sourdough timer, a chord finder),
something for your community (a church rota, a club's fixtures, a food bank's opening hours),
a calm, focused version of an app you find too noisy.

description.text: Keep the first version **small**: one main screen, one core action, done beautifully. You can always add more in version 1.1.
Write it down
Before opening Xcode, write a one-page plan:

items: **The problem**, in one sentence.
**Who it is for.**
**User stories**: five to ten "I can…" sentences, like the projects in this course. Mark the three that matter most.
**The data**: your models and their properties.
**The screens**: a rough sketch of each, on paper.
**Platforms**: iPhone first? Mac too? A widget?

questions.question: What makes a good first app?

answers.text: A copy of a popular app
A small app that solves a problem you have yourself
The biggest app you can imagine

questions.why: You will use it, notice what is wrong, and finish it.

lessons.title: Capstone: build and ship it

description.text: Build the app you planned, and ship it.

There is no template and no test suite. What you have instead is everything in this course, Apple's documentation, the Swift community, and your own judgement, which has grown a great deal since your first `print`.
Work in small steps. Get the most important user story working end to end first, even if it is ugly. Then the next. Commit to Git often. Put the app on your phone early, and use it.
When it does its core job well, send it to a few friends through TestFlight. Listen more than you explain. Fix what confuses them. Then submit it to the App Store.
When it is live, you are an app developer. Congratulations, and well done.

chapters.title: Modern Apple
chapters.summary: The frameworks that make an app feel at home on iOS 27 and macOS 27: Apple Intelligence, Siri, iCloud, Liquid Glass, evaluations and sharing.

lessons.title: A session on the device

description.text: Apple Intelligence includes an on-device language model. The Foundation Models framework gives your app a `LanguageModelSession`: instructions, a prompt, and a response. Everything happens on the device, so the feature works offline and the text never leaves the Mac or iPhone.

blocks.text: Check `availability` before you show a button. A control that cannot work is worse than an honest sentence that says why.

description.text: A session is cheap to make and expensive to keep. For one question, make one session inside the task. For a conversation, keep the same session so the model remembers what it said. Sessions are not `Sendable`; keep them on the actor that uses them.

instructions.text: Build a small app with a text field, a button and a result view. Gate the button on the model's availability, create the session inside the button's task, and map `LanguageModelError` to a sentence a person can act on.

checklist: Check SystemLanguageModel.default.availability and explain each unavailable case.
Create the session inside the Task, not in the view's body.
Show the answer in a scrollable view with a copy button.
Handle cancellation when the person leaves the screen.

questions.question: Where does an on-device Foundation Models session run?
questions.why: The on-device model runs locally, works offline and keeps the prompt on the device.

questions.question: What should you do before showing an Apple Intelligence button?

answers.text: Check availability and say why when it is unavailable

questions.why: Availability differs by device, region and whether Apple Intelligence is turned on.

lessons.title: Guided generation and streaming

description.text: Asking for free text is the easy case. Asking for a Swift value is the useful one. Mark a type `@Generable` and the framework makes the model fill it in, field by field.
For a longer answer, stream it so the person sees progress: `for try await snapshot in session.streamResponse(to: prompt) { text = snapshot.content }`. Each snapshot is the text so far, not a delta.

blocks.text: Latency is mostly output tokens. Ask for the smallest structure that does the job, cap arrays with `.maximumCount`, and never ask the model for a value your code already knows.

instructions.text: Add a guided `@Generable` type to the app, give every field a `@Guide`, and print the result. Then stream the same request and replace the text as snapshots arrive.

checklist: Use @Generable and @Guide on every field the model fills.
Cap arrays and ranges so the output cannot run away.
Use .greedy sampling for a stable, checkable result.
Show a progress state while the model works.

description.text: Some requests need more reasoning or a larger context than the on-device model has. Private Cloud Compute runs the same Apple Foundation Models on Apple's servers, with the same privacy promises, and returns to your app through the same `LanguageModelSession` API.

PCC is not a free upgrade you can switch on. It needs Apple's managed entitlement `com.apple.developer.private-cloud-compute`, granted to your team. It also needs a network, has a daily quota, and can fail with `networkFailure`, `quotaLimitReached` or `serviceUnavailable`.

blocks.text: Ship on device first. Keep PCC behind a setting, check its availability, and fall back to the on-device model when the network or the quota says no.

instructions.text: Decide which feature in your app genuinely needs more reasoning. Keep it on device by default and add a PCC path only behind the entitlement, an availability check and a person's choice.

questions.question: What does Private Cloud Compute require that the on-device model does not?

answers.text: Apple's managed entitlement and a network

questions.why: The entitlement is granted by Apple, and requests travel to Apple's PCC infrastructure.

questions.question: What should happen when the PCC quota is reached?

answers.text: Fall back to the on-device model and say so

questions.why: A quota is a reason to use the device, not a dead end.

lessons.title: Entities Siri can see

description.text: Siri does not read your database. It works with `AppEntity` values: a stable id, a display representation, and a query that can find them. Conform to `IndexedEntity` and the same values can appear in Spotlight.

The id must be stable across launches. A UUID made at runtime is fine; the lesson's own string id is better because the course already has one. Do the store reads on the main actor; the query itself is not main-actor isolated.

instructions.text: Make one of your app's types an `AppEntity` with a stable id and a query. Then make it an `IndexedEntity` and donate the values to Spotlight.

checklist: The id survives a relaunch and a reinstall.
displayRepresentation has a title and a useful subtitle.
The query reads the same store the window shows, on the main actor.
Spotlight indexing is off when the person turns sharing off.

lessons.title: App Shortcuts and phrases

description.text: An `AppShortcut` is a phrase Siri can match without the person setting anything up. Every phrase contains `\(.applicationName)`. Only an `AppEntity` or `AppEnum` may be interpolated; a plain `String` cannot be, because Siri has nothing to match it against.

A background intent returns a value and a dialog: `some IntentResult & ProvidesDialog & ReturnsValue<Int>`. A foreground intent changes what is on screen. Pick the mode that matches what the person asked for, and never do both by accident.

blocks.text: Test each phrase on a device. The Shortcuts app is not Siri: a shortcut can work while the spoken phrase does not.

instructions.text: Add two shortcuts: one that opens the next lesson, and one that answers a question without opening the app. Speak both phrases on a device.

checklist: Every phrase contains \(.applicationName).
No String parameter appears inside a phrase.
The background intent returns a value and a dialog.
The foreground intent uses .foreground and opens the right screen.

lessons.title: SwiftData in iCloud

description.text: SwiftData can mirror a model to the person's private CloudKit database with one configuration. The price is a set of rules: every stored property has a default, no unique constraints, and relationships are optional.

Open the container once per process. Two containers on the same file sync everything twice. In an unsigned build there is no iCloud entitlement, and CloudKit without it traps on a background queue, so keep a local fallback and say which one is in use.

blocks.text: Adding a property is a schema change. Give it a default, run the app once with the schema-initialisation flag, then deploy the schema to Production in CloudKit Console. Renaming or removing a property after that is not possible.

instructions.text: Add a second model to a SwiftData app and sync it through the private database. Open the CloudKit Console, check the record type, and deploy the schema.

checklist: Every property has a default or is optional.
No @Attribute(.unique) and no #Unique.
One ModelContainer for the whole process.
cloudKitDatabase: .none for previews, demos and tests.
The schema is deployed to Production before release.

description.text: Progress belongs in SwiftData. A handful of preferences can live in `NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore`, Apple's key-value store in iCloud. It is small, last-writer-wins, and perfect for an accent colour or a text size, not for a course record.

blocks.text: Keep the local `UserDefaults` copy as the source for the current launch. KVS can be slow to arrive and can be empty on a new device.

questions.question: What belongs in iCloud key-value storage?
questions.why: KVS is small, last-writer-wins and not a database.

questions.question: What should you do when a KVS value arrives from another device?

answers.text: Update the UI and keep a local copy

questions.why: Observe didChangeExternallyNotification and apply the change.

description.text: Liquid Glass is a functional layer, not a decoration. It belongs on controls and navigation that float above content: toolbars, tab bars, a floating Run button. It does not belong on every list row or every card.

The `regular` variant blurs and adjusts the background so text stays legible. Use `clear` only over photos and video, where seeing the content matters more than the chrome. System controls already use glass; adding more of it by hand usually makes the screen worse.

blocks.text: On the Mac, `.buttonStyle(.glass)` on small circular toolbar buttons can render as a solid accent circle. Use `.borderless` there.

questions.question: Where does Liquid Glass belong?

answers.text: On controls and navigation above the content

questions.why: Glass separates the functional layer from the content layer.

questions.question: Which variant keeps text legible over a complex background?
questions.why: Regular blurs and adjusts luminosity; clear is for rich media.

lessons.title: Glass that moves

description.text: `GlassEffectContainer` lets nearby glass shapes merge and morph. Give each shape a `glassEffectID` in a namespace, then change the state inside `withAnimation`.
The morph is a transition, not a loop. Respect Reduce Motion: when it is on, change the state without the movement and keep the result.

instructions.text: Build a small glass control that expands into three glass chips. Animate the change, then turn Reduce Motion on and check it still makes sense.

checklist: Shapes share a GlassEffectContainer and a namespace.
Every shape has a stable glassEffectID.
The state change is inside withAnimation.
Reduce Motion removes the movement, not the function.

lessons.title: Testing an intelligent feature

description.text: A unit test asks whether code does what it says. An evaluation asks whether a model does the job well enough. Apple's Evaluations framework runs your feature over a dataset, scores each answer, and reports the aggregate. It integrates with Swift Testing through `@Test(.evaluates(...))`.

Use code-based evaluators for anything computable: counts, ranges, valid citations, required words. Use a model judge for tone and clarity, and calibrate it against your own reading. Keep hostile and empty inputs in the dataset; they are where features break.

instructions.text: Write an evaluation for one model feature in your app. Include ten ordinary inputs, two empty ones, and two hostile ones that try to give the model instructions.

checklist: The dataset covers ordinary, edge and adversarial inputs.
Code evaluators check everything that can be checked by code.
A model judge is used only for qualities code cannot measure.
The suite runs in CI and fails below an agreed score.

lessons.title: Share a milestone

description.text: A share card is a view you render to an image. Draw it with SwiftUI, render with `ImageRenderer`, wrap the PNG in a `Transferable`, and hand it to `ShareLink`. Messages, Mail and social apps all receive a real image.
Render at a size that reads in a message: 1080 by 1350 is a good 4:5 card. Keep the brand, the milestone and one number. Do not put anything private on it without the person choosing to share.

blocks.text: Avoid force unwraps in shipping code. If rendering fails, show a sentence instead of an empty card.

instructions.text: Make a share card for something your app already tracks. Render it, share it to Messages, and check it at thumbnail size.

checklist: The card is readable at 200 points wide.
The image is a real PNG, not a screenshot of the screen.
Nothing private is included without a choice.
Rendering failure shows a sentence, not a crash.

lessons.title: Live Activities

description.text: A Live Activity puts the state of something ongoing on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island. It is not a notification and it is not a widget. You describe the attributes once, then update the content as the state changes.
Update only when the state genuinely changes; each update costs battery. End the activity when the work is done. A Live Activity can receive push updates, but it does not need a server to be useful.

instructions.text: Add a Live Activity for a long-running piece of work in your app. Start it, update it twice, and end it. Check the Lock Screen and the Dynamic Island.

checklist: The attributes are small and stable; the changing values are in ContentState.
The activity ends when the work ends.
Updates are meaningful, not a timer.
The Lock Screen and Dynamic Island both read well.
